entry.title: The Recipe Book Behind Zephyr and SmolLM3 - Inside huggingface/alignment-handbook

link.title: The Recipe Book Behind Zephyr and SmolLM3 - Inside huggingface/alignment-handbook

entry.content:
Some repositories impress with volume, and some with restraint. The Alignment Handbook, from Lewis Tunstall, Edward Beeching, Nathan Lambert, Nazneen Rajani, Shengyi Huang, Kashif Rasul, Alvaro Bartolome, Carlos M. Patino, Alexander M. Rush, and Thomas Wolf at Hugging Face, is emphatically the second kind. It is the codebase that produced Zephyr-7B-beta - one of the most downloaded fine-tuned chat models of its moment on the Hub - and later the post-training recipe behind SmolLM3-3B, yet its entire Python surface is barely 1,250 lines: three launch scripts that mostly wire arguments together, a four-module support package, and one test file. The real payload is the recipes directory: versioned YAML files that record every hyperparameter, dataset split, and accelerate setting behind each released model, with a technical report at arXiv 2310.16944 documenting the results.

As always in this series, what follows is an educational tour of published source code.

Overview: accelerate configs and Slurm launchers feed the three training scripts; a thin alignment package validates dataset mixtures and loads models; each script wraps one TRL trainer; recipe YAMLs drive everything; release tooling ships checkpoints to the Hub.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • scripts/sft.py is the 174-line supervised fine-tuning entry point: main at line 54 loads data at 87, tokenizer at 91, and model at 96, falls back to ChatML when the tokenizer has no template at 98-100, and builds TRL’s SFTTrainer at 105-112.
  • scripts/dpo.py, 159 lines, builds the policy and a second frozen reference model with two get_model calls at lines 100-101, then hands both to DPOTrainer at 122-130 - the same implicit-reward loss we toured in direct-preference-optimization, now production-wrapped.
  • scripts/orpo.py, 158 lines, is the single-stage variant: ORPOTrainer at line 122 takes no reference model, fusing SFT and preference alignment into one run.
  • src/alignment/configs.py extends TRL’s argument dataclasses: DatasetConfig at line 37, DatasetMixtureConfig at 48, and ScriptArguments at 57 whose post_init at 88 validates mixtures and enforces consistent column sets at 122-130.
  • src/alignment/data.py is the 79-line heart of the mixture API: get_dataset at line 26 loads each entry, subsamples by weight at 52-56, concatenates and reshuffles at 61-62, and optionally carves a test split at 65-68.
  • src/alignment/model_utils.py holds get_tokenizer at line 23 - which can override the chat template at 31-32 - and get_model at 37, resolving dtype and quantization at 39-42 and disabling the KV cache under gradient checkpointing at 48.
  • recipes/zephyr-7b-beta/dpo/config_full.yaml is the artifact that made the repo famous: it starts from the SFT checkpoint, mixes ultrafeedback_binarized preference splits, and sets beta 0.01 with learning rate 5e-7.
  • recipes/smollm3/sft/sft.yaml is the modern extreme: 228 lines declaring 26 weighted smoltalk2 sources, packing with the ffd strategy at length 65536, assistant-only loss, and five epochs.

Why You Need This

Frameworks are places where options go to hide. LLaMA-Factory and axolotl expose hundreds of switches because they must serve every use case; the Handbook inverts that - it serves exactly one use case, replicating published results, and strips everything else away. Each script is a legible main function you can read top to bottom in two minutes: set seed, load data, load tokenizer, load model, construct trainer, train, save, push. Where ms-swift routes dozens of model families through registries and OpenRLHF distributes a controller over Ray, the Handbook’s entire distribution story is three accelerate config files and a 176-line Slurm script. Reading it teaches you what a TRL training run actually consists of when no framework is watching.

The mixture API deserves its own study because data blending turned out to be the quiet superpower of every model this repo shipped. The Zephyr SFT recipe mixes ultrachat_200k train and test splits with equal weights; the SmolLM3 recipe blends 26 sources with weights from 1.0 down to 0.02, balancing everyday chats against function calling, long-context tasks, and reasoning traces in both think and no-think variants. The implementation is deliberately simple - shuffle, take a weight fraction, concatenate, reshuffle - and tests/test_data.py pins the arithmetic: three 100-row datasets weighted 0.5, 0.3, and 0.2 yield exactly 90 train and 10 test rows, asserted at lines 44-45. If you have ever wondered how recipe authors express “mostly instruction data, a dash of math,” this is the answer, and it transfers directly to your own training runs, whether you fine-tune full weights with deepspeed ZeRO-3 or bolt peft adapters on through the same get_peft_config call at sft.py line 111.

Finally, the Handbook is the missing link between the algorithm papers this series has covered and the models you actually download. The DPO recipe here is the industrial version of the reference implementation - same loss, but with checkpoint resumption, Hub push, model cards tagged alignment-handbook at sft.py line 145, and the generation config’s eos_token_id synced to the tokenizer at lines 136-137 to prevent unbounded generation. The ORPO script shows the alternative trade - skip the reference model entirely - while the evaluation guidance in scripts/README.md points at MT-Bench, AlpacaEval, and Chatbot Arena, a reminder that lm-evaluation-harness scores are only one lens on a chat model. The repo even ships its own release tooling, because a recipe you cannot re-version is a recipe you cannot trust.

Detail: three script mains share the parser, mixture API, and model loaders; each wraps a different TRL trainer; recipe YAMLs parameterize everything from Zephyr’s two stages to SmolLM3’s 26-corpus blend; release tooling closes the versioning loop.

The scripts are deliberately near-identical, and the diffs are where the interesting decisions live. All three begin with set_seed at line 56 (sft.py), checkpoint detection via get_last_checkpoint at 78-82, and the same three-part TrlParser at the bottom - ScriptArguments, a task config, and TRL’s ModelConfig - so every recipe is one YAML deep. sft.py’s signature moves: when the tokenizer lacks a chat template, setup_chat_format retrofits the model’s embedding matrix for ChatML special tokens at 98-100; before saving, eos_token_id is written into both generation_config and config at 136-137; and on the main process only, use_cache is switched back on at 150-151 since training disabled it for gradient checkpointing. dpo.py instead builds two models - policy at line 100, reference at 101 - falls back to eos as the pad token at 103-104, carries an ignore_bias_buffers switch at 105-109 that tells DDP to skip boolean buffers (a workaround for Flash Attention asserts in distributed DPO), and strips the messages column at 114-117 so the trainer sees only chosen/rejected pairs. orpo.py removes the reference model altogether, matching the method’s single-stage design documented in its docstring with max_length 2048.

The mixture chain is three short files acting in concert. ScriptArguments at configs.py line 57 accepts either dataset_name or a dataset_mixture dict; post_init at 88 rejects configs with neither, coerces the raw dict into DatasetConfig entries at 99-112 - each carrying id, config name, split, a columns whitelist, and a weight - and then insists at 122-130 that every entry whitelists the same column names, because concatenation would otherwise fail late and cryptically. get_dataset in data.py takes it from there: the single-dataset branch at lines 35-37 is a plain load_dataset call, while the mixture branch at 38-76 loads each source with its split at 45-49, applies select_columns at 50-51, implements weights as shuffle-then-select(range(int(len(ds) * weight))) at 52-56, concatenates at 61, applies one final seeded shuffle at 62, and either returns a DatasetDict with a train_test_split at 65-68 or wraps everything as a lone train split at 73-74. The tests lock the semantics in at three weight regimes, including the fractional case where 70 plus 40 rows become 99 train and 11 test at lines 87-105.

The model layer is fifty-seven lines that encode real distributed-training judgment. get_tokenizer at model_utils.py line 23 loads with the model revision and trust_remote_code flags from ModelConfig, then applies the recipe’s chat_template override at 31-32 - which is how Zephyr’s custom template and SmolLM3’s reasoning-aware template, both stored as YAML strings inside the recipes, reach the tokenizer without any code changes. get_model at line 37 resolves torch_dtype from the string at 39-41, asks TRL for a bitsandbytes quantization config at 42, and assembles model_kwargs at 43-51: attention implementation passthrough, use_cache forced False whenever gradient_checkpointing is on at 48, and a kbit device map only when quantization is active at 49. That last detail is the difference between a QLoRA run that colocates quantized weights correctly across GPUs and one that silently double-loads.

The recipes are the repo’s true deliverables, and comparing them is a history of post-training itself. Zephyr-7B-beta’s SFT config points at Mistral-7B-v0.1 with flash_attention_2, a learning rate of 2e-5 for one epoch, sequences of 2048 tokens, and a per-device batch of 16 on the eight-GPU ZeRO-3 node declared in recipes/accelerate_configs/zero3.yaml - which sets zero_stage 3, zero3_init_flag, and zero3_save_16bit_model at lines 7-9; its DPO config then starts from the resulting Hub checkpoint with beta 0.01 and lr 5e-7, the low-beta regime the Zephyr report found best. The fsdp.yaml alternative chooses FULL_SHARD with TRANSFORMER_BASED_WRAP and BACKWARD_PRE prefetch - the same strategy family as the direct-preference-optimization reference - plus SHARDED_STATE_DICT and cpu_ram_efficient_loading. SmolLM3’s sft.yaml pushes the mixture API to its limit: 26 entries from smoltalk2 with weights like 0.02 for OpenThoughts3 reasoning traces and 0.5 for magpie-ultra, assistant_only_loss true, packing_strategy ffd at 65536 tokens, liger kernel enabled, cosine_with_min_lr at min_lr_rate 0.1, and a ddp_timeout of 18000 seconds because tokenizing that blend takes hours. SmolLM3’s DPO stage then runs loss_type apo_zero with beta 0.05 and padding_free true, while smollm2 shows the small-model contrast: beta 0.5, three epochs, tensorboard plus wandb. The Slurm launcher ties it together - it greps gradient_accumulation_steps out of the chosen config at line 90, reserves the last node as a vLLM server when use_vllm is set at 117-130, exports NCCL_ASYNC_ERROR_HANDLING at 133, and sruns the accelerate command across nodes at 140-167.

Release discipline rounds out the design. src/alignment/release.py keeps a REPLACE_PATTERNS table at lines 22-36 that rewrites the version string in four files at once - init.py, setup.py, CITATION.cff, and the README citation block - with pre_release_work at 73 refusing to patch from a dev branch at 77-78 and post_release_work at 95 bumping to the next dev0. setup.py carries the pinning that makes recipes reproducible: trl>=0.19.1, transformers>=4.53.3, torch>=2.6.0, peft>=0.16.0, deepspeed>=0.17.2, and liger-kernel>=0.6.0 among the deps at lines 43-73, with the package itself named alignment-handbook at version 0.4.0.dev0. It is a small thing until you try to reproduce a 2023 result on a 2026 stack - then the recipe that pins its world is the only one that still works.

From Install to a Replicated Zephyr

The README and scripts/README.md give a five-command path from nothing to a replicated Zephyr-7B-beta (commands abridged):

uv venv handbook --python 3.11 && source handbook/bin/activate
uv pip install torch==2.6.0 --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu126
uv pip install . && uv pip install "flash-attn==2.7.4.post1" --no-build-isolation
huggingface-cli login
# Stage 1 - SFT on 8 GPUs with ZeRO-3
ACCELERATE_LOG_LEVEL=info accelerate launch --config_file recipes/accelerate_configs/zero3.yaml \
  scripts/sft.py --config recipes/zephyr-7b-beta/sft/config_full.yaml
# Stage 2 - DPO from the SFT checkpoint
ACCELERATE_LOG_LEVEL=info accelerate launch --config_file recipes/accelerate_configs/zero3.yaml \
  scripts/dpo.py --config recipes/zephyr-7b-beta/dpo/config_full.yaml

Every parameter can be overridden on the command line - the docs suggest scaling batch size with GPU count to keep the global batch, and recipes will push straight to your Hub namespace by default.

Honest limits: the scripts are thin by design, so anything TRL does not expose - custom losses, curriculum scheduling, multi-stage reward modeling - means editing library code, not adding a config; the mixture API loads and concatenates full datasets in memory, which large blends only survive through the streaming-free weight trick it does not implement; the Slurm launcher is tuned for the Hugging Face cluster and says so; chat model evaluation leans on GPT-4 judges (MT-Bench, AlpacaEval) whose biases the README itself flags, including a taste for GPT-distilled models; and the repo is Apache 2.0 code wrapping libraries that move fast, so the exact torch, transformers, and trl pins are not suggestions - the recipes will silently change behavior without them.
entry.summary: A source tour of the Alignment Handbook: a thin TRL wrapper, the dataset mixture API, the Zephyr-7B-beta two-stage recipe, SmolLM3's 26-corpus blend, and the release tooling that ships models to the Hub.

entry.title: One YAML, Every Fine-Tune - Inside axolotl-ai-cloud/axolotl

link.title: One YAML, Every Fine-Tune - Inside axolotl-ai-cloud/axolotl

entry.content:
Fine-tuning an open model used to mean writing a training script: dataset glue, tokenizer surgery, trainer arguments, sharding flags, and a prayer that the checkpoint resumes. Axolotl replaces the script with a single YAML file and a codebase whose whole architecture exists to translate that YAML into a correct, memory-efficient training run. The result is one of the most widely used fine-tuning frameworks in the open-source world, and its source is a masterclass in how to layer configuration, data, and distributed training without letting any of them tangle. Version 0.21.1 under an Apache-2.0 license, it currently spans roughly 750 Python modules under its src tree, covering everything from classic Alpaca prompt formats to NVFP4 MoE LoRA kernels and asynchronous GRPO rollouts.

What makes the codebase worth reading is that it is honest about the messy parts. Every performance trick you have heard about - sample packing, flash attention swaps, FSDP2 with 4-bit bases, fused Liger kernels - lives here as an actual patch or plugin with clear seams, not as a blog diagram. You can trace one YAML key from the schema that validates it, through the loader that acts on it, to the trainer mixin that consumes it. As always in this series, what follows is an educational tour of published source code.

Overview: the CLI and config layer feeds dataset machinery and model loading; the trainer core consumes packed batches while patches and plugins reshape the model in between.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • cli/main.py is the dispatcher whose main at line 529 wires every subcommand from train to preprocess to merge to cloud launches.
  • utils/config/init.py at 636 lines reads the YAML, applies defaults and plugin additions, and hands it to validation.
  • utils/schemas/config.py defines AxolotlInputConfig at line 196, a 2240-line pydantic schema that is effectively the framework’s contract with users.
  • utils/data/sft.py starts at prepare_datasets line 49 and assembles raw, tokenized, and shuffled datasets for supervised runs.
  • prompt_strategies/chat_template.py implements ChatTemplateStrategy at line 308, turning chat rows into masked label tensors.
  • utils/samplers/multipack.py provides MultipackBatchSampler at line 252, the best-fit-decreasing bin packer that keeps sequences together.
  • loaders/model.py is ModelLoader at line 209, 1468 lines handling quantization configs, device maps, and attention impl selection.
  • train.py closes the loop with train at line 703: setup, execute, save, model card, plugin teardown.

Why You Need This

If you have read our tours of peft, accelerate, or deepspeed, you know the individual parts: adapters, sharding, ZeRO stages. Axolotl is the orchestration layer that binds them behind one config file, and reading it shows you what integration actually costs. The repo does not just call PEFT’s get_peft_model; it patches PEFT’s parameter wrappers, seeds adapter initialization deterministically, and validates that a saved adapter matches the patterns you asked for. Those are the failure modes you only discover after your third night-long run dies at step 4000.

It is also the best available map of the 2025-2026 fine-tuning frontier in executable form. QLoRA on FSDP2 without a full-precision replica per GPU, NVFP4 MoE adapters via custom Triton kernels, selective activation checkpointing with CPU offload, asynchronous GRPO with a rollout producer - each landed as a self-contained module you can read in isolation. When a technique confuses you in a paper, the odds are good this repo contains the production version of it. Our torchtitan tour showed a clean-room trainer; axolotl shows the same ideas bolted onto the Hugging Face ecosystem where most practitioners actually live.

Finally, the plugin architecture is a lesson in extension design. Liger kernels, the ScatterMoE LoRA library, evaluation hooks, and even cloud launchers all enter through the same BasePlugin contract, getting called at pre-config-load, pre-model-load, post-model-load, and post-train phases. Nothing core knows Liger exists; the patch manager just asks registered plugins to do their worst at defined moments. If you maintain any training tool and want to stop merging every user request into core, this is the pattern to steal.

Detailed view: entry and config, dataset machinery, model and adapter loading, the trainer core, RL and preference trainers, and the patch and kernel layer.

Start at the entry, because the config is the product. cli/train.py defines do_cli at line 88 and do_train at line 37; the config path lands in utils/config/init.py which merges plugin-added keys before utils/schemas/config.py validates against AxolotlInputConfig at line 196. The schema is worth an evening: every knob from sequence_len to flash_attention is declared with types and defaults, and a capability-aware subclass AxolotlConfigWCapabilities at line 1939 cross-references the declared attention implementation against the installed hardware before a single GPU is touched. When validation fails you get a pydantic error pointing at the exact key, not a CUDA OOM nine hours later.

The dataset machinery is the second act. utils/data/sft.py loads raw datasets at line 319, applies the selected strategy through prompt_strategies/chat_template.py whose ChatTemplateStrategy at line 308 builds input and label tensors from any Jinja chat template, and persists the tokenized result so runs after the first skip straight to loading at line 268. The strategy ABCs live in prompt_tokenizers.py with PromptTokenizingStrategy at line 43, and the legacy Alpaca family at line 162 shows how train-on-input masking works. For RL runs the parallel module utils/data/rl.py at 528 lines prepares preference and prompt datasets instead.

The packing story is where axolotl earns its throughput. utils/samplers/multipack.py implements MultipackBatchSampler at line 252: sequence lengths come in, ffd_check at line 33 validates the bin estimate, pack_group at line 69 does best-fit-decreasing, and generate_batches at line 378 emits index batches whose padding waste is reported by efficiency at line 597. The sampler plugs into AxolotlTrainer through _create_multipack_sampler at line 363 of core/trainers/base.py, and the matching collator V2BatchSamplerDataCollatorForSeq2Seq at line 213 of utils/collators/batching.py pads to the batch max rather than a global max. A monkeypatch teaches the stock HF Trainer about these variable-length batches so loss normalization counts real tokens, a detail that silently skews results if ignored.

Model loading is a 1468-line negotiation with reality. ModelLoader.load at line 313 of loaders/model.py runs pre-model-load patches, picks device map via _set_device_map_config at line 922, quantization via _set_quantization_config at line 1006, and attention via _set_attention_config at line 1105, then _build_model at line 1243 actually constructs the model and _build_adapters at line 727 attaches LoRA through loaders/adapter.py whose load_lora at line 414 and find_all_linear_names at line 60 decide what gets adapters. The deepest magic is monkeypatch/accelerate/fsdp2.py: fsdp2_load_full_state_dict at line 183 shards a full checkpoint across ranks while keeping 4-bit quantized parameters intact, fsdp2_prepare_model at line 583 applies activation checkpointing, and the QLoRA companion monkeypatch/fsdp2_qlora.py makes adapters trainable on the sharded quantized base - the CPU-staged loading that lets you fine-tune models bigger than any single GPU.

On top sit the trainers and plugins. AxolotlTrainer at line 114 of core/trainers/base.py overrides compute_loss at line 771 for proper token-level normalization and composes mixins from core/trainers/mixins/packing.py. RL lives in core/trainers/grpo/trainer.py with AxolotlGRPOTrainer at line 57 and a context-parallel variant at line 89 whose _generate_and_score_completions at line 297 does the rollout-scoring dance, while core/trainers/grpo/async_trainer.py builds a full producer-consumer system - AsyncDataProducer at line 368, RolloutDataset at line 529, AsyncGRPOTrainer at line 832 - so generation overlaps training. Plugins enter through integrations/base.py; LigerPlugin at line 34 of integrations/liger/plugin.py swaps fused kernels in pre_model_load at line 114, and KernelsPlugin at line 146 of integrations/kernels/plugin.py routes MoE adapters to the ScatterMoE library’s grouped kernels while registering house Triton ops like the swiglu in kernels/swiglu.py.

What happens after the last step matters just as much, and the post-training exit ramps are built in. train at line 703 of train.py finishes with save_trained_model at line 274, which handles the FSDP merge-and-rename path (a helper at line 252 renames merged shards to adapter form), writes the model card at line 488, and calls PluginManager.post_train so plugins can unload or upload. From there the CLI takes over: cli/merge_lora.py collapses adapters into base weights with a memory-efficient variant at line 119, and the export command drives utils/gguf.py whose export_gguf at line 149 resolves llama.cpp binaries, preflights the vocab and template at line 89, and quantizes straight to a deployable GGUF for llama.cpp or Ollama. A fine-tune that ends in a serving-ready file without leaving the tool is the actual deliverable most users want.

From Install to Fine-Tuned Model

The README’s uv-first install and one-command train:

curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh
export UV_TORCH_BACKEND=cu130
uv venv --python 3.12
uv pip install torch==2.14.0 torchvision
uv pip install --no-build-isolation axolotl[deepspeed]
axolotl fetch examples
axolotl train examples/llama-3/lora-1b.yml

The same path programmatically, which is how notebooks and sweeps drive it:

from axolotl.cli.train import do_cli

do_cli(config="examples/llama-3/lora-1b.yml")

Change a few keys - base_model, learning_rate, lora_target_modules, flash_attention: true - and the identical command fine-tunes a different architecture; add rl: grpo with a reward function and the same entrypoint switches to the GRPO trainer.

Honest limits: axolotl’s breadth is also its surface area - the monkeypatch and model_support trees track upstream Hugging Face and torch releases closely, so pinning versions matters more here than in smaller tools. The config schema documents most keys, but exotic combinations (NVFP4 MoE plus context parallelism, say) carry caveats that only the docs’ support matrix admits to. And like every YAML-driven trainer, it will happily train a mediocre model on a mediocre dataset; no framework validates that your data was worth the GPU hours.
entry.summary: A source tour of axolotl, the configuration-driven fine-tuning framework: pydantic config validation, prompt strategies, multipack bin-packing, FSDP2 QLoRA patches, plugin integrations, and GRPO trainers.

entry.title: Your Language Model Is Secretly a Reward Model - Inside eric-mitchell/direct-preference-optimization

link.title: Your Language Model Is Secretly a Reward Model - Inside eric-mitchell/direct-preference-optimization

entry.content:
In May 2023 a Stanford team - Rafael Rafailov, Archit Sharma, Eric Mitchell, Christopher D. Manning, Stefano Ermon, and Chelsea Finn - posted “Direct Preference Optimization: Your Language Model Is Secretly a Reward Model” (arXiv 2305.18290), and the title carried the whole idea: instead of training a separate reward model and then squeezing a policy against it with reinforcement learning, DPO derives a closed-form mapping from an optimal KL-constrained policy back to its implicit reward, and rewrites the entire alignment objective as one classification loss over preference pairs. No PPO rollouts, no reward-model head, no KL penalty coefficients to babysit. This repository is the paper’s reference implementation: four Python files totaling about 1,224 lines - no framework, no plugin registry, just the loss, three trainer classes, and loaders for the three preference corpora the experiments used.

As always in this series, what follows is an educational tour of published source code.

Overview: a Hydra entry point resolves configs and builds policy plus frozen reference; three dataset loaders normalize their corpora into one dict schema; tokenization builds left-padded chosen/rejected pairs; the loss function branches over DPO, IPO, and cDPO; and three trainers share the concatenated forward while diverging in sharding strategy.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • train.py is the 118-line entry point: the hydra main at line 48 validates the composed config with missing_keys at 55, builds the policy at 83-84 and disables its dropout at 85, builds a frozen reference model at 87-92 for DPO and IPO, loads SFT archives at 96-103, and spawns one worker per GPU with mp.spawn at 111.
  • config/config.yaml holds the defaults - learning rate 5e-7 with RMSprop, 150 warmup steps, max_length 512 against max_prompt_length 256, batch_size 4, eval_every 20000, and trainer: BasicTrainer - while the loss and model subtrees override it per experiment.
  • preference_datasets.py, 386 lines, normalizes three corpora into one schema: get_hh at line 120 for Anthropic/hh-rlhf, get_shp at 85 for stanfordnlp/SHP, and get_se at 46 for StackExchange preferences, each yielding per-prompt dicts of responses, pairs, and sft_target enforced by an assert at 174.
  • tokenize_batch_element turns a pair into tensors: EOS asserts at 229-231 and appends at 233-237, keep_start/keep_end truncation at 242-248, and prompt labels masked to -100 at 258-261.
  • get_batch_iterator is the reproducible DataLoader factory: it shuffles under TemporarilySeededRandom at 315-316 and defaults to keep_end truncation for hh-rlhf at 319.
  • preference_loss is the whole paper in 40 lines: the policy-vs-reference log-ratio gap at lines 70-76, an IPO branch at 78-79, a label-smoothed cDPO branch at 81-82, and the implicit reward margins returned at 84-85.
  • _get_batch_logps converts one forward pass into per-sequence log probabilities - shift at 103, padding mask at 105, gather of log-softmax at 110, token-average at 112-115 - while concatenated_inputs at 118 stacks chosen and rejected rows into a single padded batch.
  • The trainer trio: BasicTrainer runs one process over a naively split model, FSDPTrainer adds full sharding with activation checkpointing, and TensorParallelTrainer shards every linear layer through the tensor-parallel package.

Why You Need This

Every alignment toolbox this series has toured ships a DPO mode, and all of them implement the same closed-form loss that lives in this repo’s 545-line trainers.py. TRL turned DPOTrainer into a one-liner, OpenRLHF and LMFlow list it among their aligner family, and ms-swift wires it into dozens of model types - yet the mathematics they configure from YAML is exactly what preference_loss at line 45 writes out: beta, label smoothing, reference-free mode, and the IPO variant are four branches of one function, not four separate systems. If you have ever wondered what actually changes when you flip loss=dpo to loss=ipo, this file answers it in forty lines you can hold in your head.

The repo also teaches the unglamorous mechanics that papers skip and production frameworks hide behind abstractions: the left-padding collate trick that makes right-padded generations scoreable, the EOS-append asserts that catch silent tokenizer bugs before they poison training, the -100 label masking that stanford-alpaca uses the same way, and the concatenated forward that scores chosen and rejected responses in a single pass - which the comment at trainers.py lines 213-219 notes is faster under FSDP, the same sharding approach axolotl and deepspeed users run alongside peft adapters and accelerate launchers. These details are precisely where first attempts at custom preference-training code go wrong, and here each one occupies a handful of auditable lines.

Finally, it is the cleanest available reference for the two-stage recipe - supervised fine-tuning to get the policy on-distribution, then preference learning from the SFT archive - that every downstream toolbox reproduces, from llama-factory stage configs to unsloth notebooks. Because the repo pins exact dependency versions and documents measured runtimes (about 1h30 for SFT and 2h45 for DPO on Pythia 2.8B across four A100s), it doubles as a reproducibility yardstick in a field where lm-evaluation-harness scores are only as meaningful as the recipe that produced the checkpoint.

Detail: loaders converge on the {responses, pairs, sft_target} schema; tokenization and collation build left-padded, label-masked pair batches; preference_loss branches over DPO, IPO, and cDPO; and the three trainers share the concatenated forward while diverging in distribution strategy.

The data half of the repo is a study in normalization. get_hh at line 120 loads Anthropic/hh-rlhf at 142 and splits each chosen/rejected transcript with split_prompt_and_responses at 145, leaning on extract_anthropic_prompt at 14, which rfinds the last “\n\nAssistant:” marker at 17. get_shp at line 85 loads stanfordnlp/SHP at 92 and keeps only candidate pairs whose score ratio is at least 2 (lines 104-106), orienting each pair from labels==1 at 109. get_se at line 46 loads HuggingFaceH4/stack-exchange-preferences at 52, strips HTML with strip_html_tags at 22 - carefully preserving code blocks at lines 34-38 - and enumerates every answer pair ordered by pm_score at 74-77. Each prompt’s sft_target is its best response: the chosen reply for hh (line 158), the top-scored answer for shp and se (lines 81 and 114), so the same loaders double as SFT data sources. get_dataset at 163 dispatches by name and hard-asserts the three-key schema at 174.

Tokenization is where pairs become tensors, and tokenize_batch_element at line 214 guards every step. It asserts the chosen and rejected prompts are identical at 229-231, appends the EOS token to both responses at 233-237, truncates with keep_start or keep_end modes at 242-248 (responses get their own pass at 251-253), and masks prompt labels to -100 at 258-261 so the loss only flows through completions. get_collate_fn at 180 implements the left-padding trick: prompt tensors are reversed at line 192, padded, then flipped back at 205-206 so padding sits on the left side of the prompt - the layout autoregressive scoring needs when batch rows must share a right edge. Attention masks pad with 0 at 200 and labels with -100 at 198. get_batch_iterator at 280 seeds each epoch’s shuffle inside TemporarilySeededRandom from utils.py at line 156, invoked at 315-316 so the permutation is reproducible without leaking the seed into global state, picks keep_end truncation for hh at 319, and serves either preference pairs or sft-only batches at 341-353.

The loss function reads like the paper’s equation section made executable. preference_loss at line 45 takes four log-probability vectors; lines 70-71 form the policy and reference log-ratios, line 76 subtracts them into logits, and the reference_free flag at 73-74 zeroes the reference term for ablations. Plain DPO is negative logsigmoid of beta times logits; the IPO branch at 78-79 swaps the logsigmoid for a squared term, (logits - 1/(2*beta))**2, citing arXiv 2310.12036; the cDPO branch at 81-82 mixes two logsigmoid terms weighted by label_smoothing, citing the conservativeness note hosted at ericmitchell.ai/cdpo.pdf and equation 7 of the DPO paper. Lines 84-85 return the implicit chosen and rejected rewards so training logs can track margins and accuracy. Feeding it, _get_batch_logps at line 90 shifts labels at 103, builds the padding mask at 105, gathers token log-probabilities from log_softmax at 110, and averages per sequence at 112-115. concatenated_inputs at line 118 pads chosen and rejected rows to a shared max_length at 127 with pad values -100 and 0 at 131, then concatenates them at 138-141 - doubling the batch once instead of running two forward passes.

BasicTrainer at line 145 is the single-process reference loop. Its train method at 272 builds the optimizer with getattr(torch.optim, self.config.optimizer) at 276 - RMSprop per the defaults - attaches a warmup LambdaLR at 277, evaluates every 20000 examples at 292, logs sample completions as wandb tables at 299, checkpoints under step-{example_counter} names at 350, accumulates gradients at 360-364, and clips at 369 through clip_gradient at 397. get_batch_samples at 182 wraps FSDP.summon_full_params at 186 so sampling sees unsharded weights. The forward path is concatenated_forward at 210, whose comment at 213-219 explains the single-pass choice is faster for FSDP; get_batch_metrics at 223 branches on the loss name at 229-242 and reports reward_accuracies at 244. save at 415 writes policy.pt, optimizer.pt, and scheduler.pt at 419-427.

FSDPTrainer at line 430 is where the same loop meets distributed state. It asserts a block_name at 439 and builds transformer_auto_wrap_policy at 441-442 so each decoder layer shards independently; it selects ShardingStrategy.FULL_SHARD at 446, CPUOffload(offload_params=False) at 447, and BackwardPrefetch.BACKWARD_PRE at 448; MixedPrecision at 457-459 honors the config dtypes; activation checkpointing wraps each block at 461-484 with CheckpointImpl.NO_REENTRANT at 476. The reference model gets its own FSDP wrapper at 486-488, gradients clip with the FSDP-native norm at 493-495, and save overrides the base to emit FULL_STATE_DICT checkpoints rank-0-only at 497-520. TensorParallelTrainer at 523 is the minimal sibling: it hands the model to tp.tensor_parallel at 533 and inherits everything else. The glue lives in train.py: worker_main at 21 picks the trainer class by name at 40, raises RLIMIT_NOFILE at 108-110 before mp.spawn at 111, and the archive loader at 96-103 restores SFT weights into both policy and reference, which may hold different dtypes since reference_dtype is resolved separately at 87-92.

The config tree itself is a Hydra composition lesson. config/config.yaml fixes trainer-agnostic defaults - one epoch, eval_every 20000, RMSprop, seed - while config/loss/dpo.yaml declares beta with Hydra’s required-key placeholder, meaning the launch will refuse to start until you choose a beta on the command line; the README suggests 0.1 to 0.5 as a starting range. config/loss/sft.yaml omits the reference-model semantics entirely, and config/model/pythia69.yaml points at EleutherAI/pythia-6.9b, names GPTNeoXLayer as the FSDP wrap target, and splits dtypes - float32 for the policy, float16 for the reference - halving reference memory at zero code cost.

From Install to a Preference-Tuned Pythia

The README’s complete example trains Pythia 2.8B on Anthropic-HH (commands abridged):

git clone https://github.com/eric-mitchell/direct-preference-optimization
cd direct-preference-optimization
python3 -m venv env && source env/bin/activate
pip install -r requirements.txt
# Stage 1 - SFT (~1h30 on 4x80GB A100s)
python -u train.py model=pythia28 datasets=[hh] loss=sft exp_name=anthropic_dpo_pythia28 \
  gradient_accumulation_steps=2 batch_size=64 eval_batch_size=32 \
  trainer=FSDPTrainer sample_during_eval=false model.fsdp_policy_mp=bfloat16
# Stage 2 - DPO from the SFT archive (~2h45 on the same machine)
python -u train.py model=pythia28 datasets=[hh] loss=dpo loss.beta=0.1 \
  exp_name=anthropic_dpo_pythia28 gradient_accumulation_steps=2 batch_size=64 eval_batch_size=32 \
  trainer=FSDPTrainer sample_during_eval=false model.fsdp_policy_mp=bfloat16 \
  model.archive=/path/to/archive/from/sft/LATEST/policy.pt

The LATEST directory under the SFT run holds the final weights, and the DPO command differs from the SFT one by exactly three flags - loss, beta, and the archive path - which is the recipe in miniature.

Honest limits: the code pins torch 2.0.1 and transformers 4.29.2, and both FSDP internals and generation APIs have moved since; sampling during evaluation is slow enough under sharding that the README recommends sample_during_eval=false; TensorParallelTrainer is flagged experimental; eval_every counts examples rather than optimizer steps; the loaders materialize the full preference dictionary in memory before batching; and FSDP runs need the file-descriptor limit raised (ulimit -n 64000). Prompts are raw “\n\nHuman: …\n\nAssistant:” strings rather than tokenizer chat templates, so adapting newer instruct models means writing your own prompt formatting in preference_datasets.py.
entry.summary: A source tour of the DPO reference implementation: three preference dataset loaders, the concatenated log-probability trick, DPO/IPO/cDPO losses in one 40-line function, and trainer classes from single GPU to FSDP.

entry.title: The Traffic Cop of the AI Gateway - The Router Inside BerriAI/litellm

link.title: The Traffic Cop of the AI Gateway - The Router Inside BerriAI/litellm

entry.content:
Every company that ships LLM features eventually writes the same program: an HTTP front door, a list of model deployments, and a way to spread traffic across them without falling over. LiteLLM, whose README bills it in one line as an “Open Source AI Gateway for 100+ LLMs. Self-hosted. Enterprise-ready,” is that program industrialized - and its industrial heart is a single Python class, the Router, that has grown to 16,046 lines inside litellm/router.py. It sits beneath a 21,775-line FastAPI proxy in litellm/proxy/proxy_server.py, weighs requests against in-flight counters and rolling latency histograms, decides which of your thirty OpenAI-compatible endpoints gets the next token, and - when that endpoint 429s at 2 a.m. - quietly cools it down, retries elsewhere, and walks a fallback list to another model group entirely. We toured the gateway’s public face when this series first visited LiteLLM; this post goes one level down, into the machinery that decides who serves the next request.

As always in this series, what follows is an educational tour of published source code.

Overview: the FastAPI proxy authenticates and enriches each request; the Router filters cooldowns, consults a strategy selector, and wraps every call in retry and fallback layers; strategy handlers track in-flight requests and latency; failures feed the cooldown cache; the chosen deployment is bridged to the provider.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • litellm/proxy/proxy_server.py is the front door: proxy_startup_event at line 1399 wires Prisma, health checks, and the shared aiohttp session into globals, while the chat route at 12710 stamps key, team, and org ids into request metadata before handing off to ProxyBaseLLMRequestProcessing at 12759.
  • litellm/proxy/auth/user_api_key_auth.py, 4,731 lines, is the dependency injected into every route: user_api_key_auth at line 4186 accepts six different credential headers at 4188-4193 and runs the whole auth phase inside an OpenTelemetry span opened at 4214-4216.
  • litellm/router.py is the Router class: init at line 1113 accepts the model_list and per-group settings, with allowed_fails configurable at 1405 and a full AllowedFailsPolicy dataclass path at 1560-1567.
  • acompletion at line 3127 is the async dispatch entry; it delegates to async_function_with_retries at 8537, whose first move at 8570 is a single make_call attempt and whose failure path re-fetches healthy deployments at 8592.
  • litellm/router_strategy/least_busy.py implements least-busy routing in 225 lines: the logging handler increments a per-deployment counter before each call at 124-125 and decrements on success or failure at 128-141, then get_available_deployments at 160-173 reads the counts from Redis or the local cache and picks the minimum.
  • litellm/router_strategy/lowest_latency.py, 555 lines, keeps a per-group latency map and, for streaming requests, switches to time-to-first-token percentiles at 451-456; deployments outside a TPM/RPM budget are dropped at 475-478, and the winner is chosen randomly among everything within a configurable buffer of the best at 492-498.
  • litellm/router_utils/cooldown_handlers.py is the failure ledger: set_cooldown_deployments at line 498 decides whether a deployment earns a cooldown, writes it into the cache at 545-550, and fires a cooldown callback task at 553-560, while async_get_cooldown_deployments at 568 is what the Router consults before every selection.
  • litellm/main.py, 9,294 lines, is the bridge the Router ultimately calls: completion at line 5328 and acompletion at 439 translate the unified OpenAI-style call into the 100+ provider-specific shapes, and litellm/cost_calculator.py prices the result with cost_per_token at line 405.

Why You Need This

A load balancer for LLMs is not a load balancer for web servers, and the Router is the clearest evidence in open source. Web requests are interchangeable; LLM requests differ by input length, so a deployment’s TPM budget is consumed at wildly different rates, and the “cost” of a failure includes all the prefill work the server already did. That is why every strategy in this codebase is a CustomLogger first and a selector second: the least-busy handler in least_busy.py only knows which deployment is free because the same class hooks log_pre_api_call at line 124 and log_success_event at 128 to maintain the counter. The latency handler likewise learns from completed calls, keeping its map keyed by model group in the shared cache. Compare that with the single-node engines this series has covered - vLLM schedules within one process and SGLang within one cluster - and the Router’s niche becomes obvious: it is the layer above them, treating each engine as a deployment with a budget and a mood.

The retry and cooldown machinery is worth reading on its own because it encodes a decade of production scar tissue. num_retries is not a single number: async_function_with_retries pops the request-level override at 8547, falls back to the Router default at 8549-8552, and then lets a per-deployment num_retries attached to the exception win at 8578-8585 - so a flaky endpoint can declare its own patience. Before any retry, the Router re-derives the healthy set at 8592 by subtracting the cooldown ledger from all deployments, an O(1) set filter at 9531-9534 rather than a loop. Cooldowns themselves are not automatic: set_cooldown_deployments consults the allowed-fails policy, and 401-style errors that no retry can fix go straight to cooldown, exactly as the docstring at 508-512 promises. If you have ever bolted tenacity onto an OpenAI client and wondered why your outage cascade got worse, this file is the missing syllabus.

Finally, the strategy dispatch shows how to make a 16,000-line class extensible without chaos. RoutingStrategy in litellm/types/router.py at line 1157 names exactly four built-in picks - least-busy, latency-based-routing, cost-based-routing, and usage-based-routing-v2 - with simple-shuffle as the default at line 139, and _select_deployment_async at 2164 is a plain match statement over those names at 2182-2215. New strategies register through routing_strategy_init at 1809, which builds a selector object and binds it to the Router. The lesson generalizes: enumerate the decisions you actually make, give each a tiny stateful module, and keep the dispatcher dumb. Teams that adopt LiteLLM behind Open WebUI or their own agents get this machinery for free; teams that hand-roll a gateway usually reimplement only the retry half and wonder why latency silently doubles during traffic spikes. And because every hook flows through CustomLogger - 1,137 lines of documented callbacks - wiring observability like Langfuse is a config entry, not a fork.

Detail: the proxy lifecycle builds the Router at startup; auth and budget gates run per request; the retry loop alternates between healthy-set filtering, strategy selection, cooldown writes, and single attempts through the provider bridge.

Start at the gateway, because everything else inherits its globals. proxy_startup_event at line 1399 declares sixteen module-level globals at 1400-1415 - prisma_client, master_key, llm_router, store_model_in_db among them - a deliberate acknowledgment that the proxy is one long-lived process per worker. It marks stale Prometheus multiprocess directories dead at 1424-1426, then runs any LITELLM_WORKER_STARTUP_HOOKS entries at 1429-1447, importing each “module.path:function_name” spec dynamically so operators can inject startup behavior without patching the image. The chat route at 12710 is thin by design: it reads the body, copies user_id, team_id, org_id, and agent_id from the authenticated key into the metadata dict at 12742-12757, and calls base_process_llm_request with route_type “acompletion” at 12761-12765. Everything that looks like business logic lives in the 21k-line file’s other 21k lines, which is exactly why the Router’s separateness matters - the same Router object serves the proxy, the SDK, and the CLI.

The selection moment deserves a slow-motion replay. After async_function_with_retries fetches the healthy list, _select_deployment_async at 2164 asks the strategy selector for a deployment, with simple-shuffle explicitly noted in the docstring at 2175-2178 as bypassing the selector machinery. For latency-based-routing, the case at 2206-2213 forwards request_kwargs, because only the caller knows whether this request streams - and that flag flips the handler to TTFT percentiles at 451-456, a detail that separates p95 prompt-processing pain from p95 time-to-first-word pain in chat UIs. The TPM/RPM guards at 475-478 reject deployments whose budgets the request would blow through, using the rpm and tpm fields any model_list entry may declare at 440-445. Then the buffer logic at 486-498 does something quietly wise: it sorts candidates by latency, keeps everything within lowest_latency_buffer of the best, and picks randomly among them - spreading load across near-equal deployments instead of hammering one winner into its own budget.

Failure handling is the second half of the same loop. When make_call at 8743 raises, the exception handler at 8573 re-enters the loop after three bookkeeping calls: _set_deployment_num_retries_on_exception at 4425 copies the deployment’s declared patience onto the error, failed-deployment stamping at 4444-4474 marks which model_info id failed so retries can skip it, and should-fail checks consult the allowed_fails counters configured back at init 1405. Cooldowns land in cooldown_cache.py - 237 lines that wrap either an in-memory TTL structure or Redis, which is what makes the whole scheme work across the proxy’s horizontal replicas. When an entire model group is exhausted, async_function_with_fallbacks at 8402 walks the configured fallback list, carrying partial usage forward so billing stays honest across the switch - the hidden-params plumbing at 3250-3282 exists precisely so a retried stream can adopt the previous attempt’s token counts.

The bridge and the bill close the tour. main.py’s completion at 5328 is where “100+ providers” becomes real: a giant dispatch by model prefix into per-provider implementations, each normalizing errors back into LiteLLM’s own exception taxonomy so the Router’s cooldown logic can treat a Bedrock ThrottlingException and an OpenAI 429 identically. cost_per_token at cost_calculator.py line 405 reads the model_prices_and_context_window.json registry that ships at the repo root - one JSON file, thousands of models, input and output rates per token - and completion_cost at 1419 assembles the final number that the proxy writes to spend logs per key, team, and user. That registry, updated by bot PRs almost daily, is the quiet moat of the project: routing, retries, and cooldowns are ideas, but knowing what a Llama 4 Maverick call costs on six clouds is data, and data compounds.

From Install to a Balanced Gateway

The README’s quickstart gets a two-deployment gateway balancing with one config (commands abridged):

pip install 'litellm[proxy]'
export LITELLM_MASTER_KEY=sk-1234
# config.yaml: two model_list entries sharing model_name "gpt-4o",
# one openai/, one azure/, plus:
#   router_settings:
#     routing_strategy: latency-based-routing
#     allowed_fails: 3
litellm --config config.yaml --port 4000
curl -X POST http://localhost:4000/v1/chat/completions \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $LITELLM_MASTER_KEY" \
  -d '{"model": "gpt-4o", "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "hi"}]}'

Both entries answer to the same public name; the Router picks per request, and /health or the cooldown debug endpoint shows which deployment is currently in timeout.

Honest limits: the Router is big because the problem is big, but the size is real - 16,046 lines with streaming fallback edges (the FallbackAwareAnthropicMessagesStream at 955 exists because mid-stream provider deaths are genuinely hard), and you should not expect to internalize it in an afternoon; the in-memory cooldown and usage caches are per-process until you attach Redis, so a single-replica deployment gets weaker guarantees than the diagrams imply; strategy quality depends on honest logging, and silent callback failures degrade routing to shuffle without errors; budget limiter enforcement (941 lines in budget_limiter.py) checks at request time, not mid-stream, so one 100k-token runaway can still overshoot a TPM cap; and the Apache 2.0 license covers the core, with several enterprise features clearly fenced off in the enterprise directory.
entry.summary: A source tour of the LiteLLM Router: latency and least-busy strategy selectors, the cooldown cache, the retry and fallback layers, and the 21,000-line FastAPI proxy that fronts 100+ LLM providers.

entry.title: 100+ Models, One Command - Inside hiyouga/LLaMA-Factory
entry.content:
Where axolotl bets on one exhaustive YAML schema, LLaMA-Factory bets on breadth: one CLI that fine-tunes over a hundred model families, one data loader that speaks every open dataset format, and one stage dispatcher that walks from continuous pretraining through supervised fine-tuning into reward modeling, PPO, DPO, and KTO. The project behind the widely cited “Unified Efficient Fine-Tuning of 100+ Language Models” paper has become the default answer to “how do I fine-tune X” for a whole generation of practitioners, and it ships a Gradio web UI so the entire journey runs from a browser. Apache-2.0 licensed, it packs its power into a surprisingly compact src tree of about 180 Python files - most of the surface area lives in a handful of genuinely enormous modules.

Those big modules are the story. A 2686-line template file encodes every supported chat format as data; a 3502-line multimodal plugin file teaches every vision-language family how to emit training rows; a 978-line trainer utilities file carries the callbacks and metrics every stage shares. Reading the repo is really reading three or four epic files plus a lattice of small workflow scripts that glue them together. As always in this series, what follows is an educational tour of published source code.

Overview: the CLI routes to a stage dispatcher; argument parsing, the template registry, and dataset processing feed model loading and the workflows; a chat facade serves the result.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • cli.py is a 31-line console entry that forwards every subcommand to the launcher.
  • launcher.py at 185 lines routes train, chat, api, export, webui, and eval to their implementations.
  • hparams/parser.py defines get_train_args at line 395, fusing five argument families into one validated tuple.
  • train/tuner.py exposes run_exp at line 163 with the stage dispatch at line 69.
  • data/loader.py loads and merges datasets via get_dataset at line 276 with caching at line 229.
  • data/template.py is the template registry: register_template at line 681 defines every supported chat format.
  • data/processor/supervised.py tokenizes rows in SupervisedDatasetProcessor at line 51.
  • model/loader.py builds the model while chat/chat_model.py serves it afterwards.

Why You Need This

Every fine-tuning tool solves the same four problems - arguments, data, model prep, training loop - and comparing implementations is the fastest way to understand the trade space. Where the axolotl tour showed a pydantic schema validating one giant YAML, LLaMA-Factory shows the Hugging Face idiom: five dataclass families (model, data, training, finetuning, generating) parsed from CLI or dict and cross-verified in _verify_model_args at line 227 of the parser. Neither is wrong; seeing both teaches you what a config system must guarantee regardless of style. The same comparison holds for adapters - this repo’s model/adapter.py implements full, freeze, and LoRA tuning side by side, next to the PEFT internals we covered in the peft tour.

The template registry deserves particular attention because it quietly carries the entire “100+ models” claim. A chat model fine-tune is useless if the prompt format does not match the pretrained format, and this file turns that compatibility problem into data: each register_template call declares system messages, user and assistant wrappers, stop tokens, and tool-call encodings for one family. New model support lands as a few lines of registration rather than a fork of the trainer - which is exactly why the README’s day-0 support table keeps filling in. If you maintain any chat-adjacent system, this is the most complete public catalog of what varies between chat formats.

Multimodal support is the other eye-opener. The data/mm_plugin.py file gives every vision-language family - LLaVA, Gemma 3, InternVL, Kimi-VL and more - a plugin that converts raw rows into the exact interleave of text and image/video tokens that family’s model class expects, including pixel-value preprocessing and image token splicing. Rather than one generic VLM loader, the repo embraces per-family reality. And when the current architecture finally hits its limits, the v1 subtree shows the rewrite: a cleaner engine split (data_engine, model_engine, base_trainer) with its own plugin system - worth reading as a case study in how projects migrate themselves.

Detailed view: entry and dispatch, argument families, the data machinery with templates and multimodal plugins, model preparation, the six stage trainers, and the inference surface.

Follow one stage end to end. llamafactory-cli train lands in launcher.py, which calls run_exp at line 163 of train/tuner.py; read_args at line 112 of hparams/parser.py accepts either a dict or command-line tokens, and get_train_args at line 395 returns the five-class tuple after _verify_model_args at line 227 rejects contradictions like a missing template. The _training_function at line 69 then dispatches: stage sft goes to run_sft at line 41 of train/sft/workflow.py, while pt, rm, ppo, dpo, and kto each have a sibling workflow - and lines 92 through 136 show optional detours into hyper-parallel, Megatron-Bridge, and Megatron-core backends when those packages are installed.

The data path inside run_sft is the loader at work. data/loader.py merges every named dataset at line 164, converts rows via data/converter.py (alpaca, sharegpt, openai formats), resolves the chat template through get_template_and_fix_tokenizer at line 819 of data/template.py, and hands rows to the processors: SupervisedDatasetProcessor at line 51 of data/processor/supervised.py builds input_ids with labels masked outside responses, its packed subclass at line 146 concatenates sequences with position-id resets, and the PairwiseDatasetProcessor at line 30 of data/processor/pairwise.py produces the chosen/rejected pairs that DPO and reward stages consume. Collators from data/collator.py finish the batches.

Model preparation is the patcher’s show. model/loader.py picks quantization through model/model_utils/quantization.py - AQLM, AWQ, GPTQ, HQQ, EETQ, and bitsandbytes variants - then model/patcher.py applies patch_config at line 365 (rope scaling, attention impl, flash-attn selection), patch_model at line 437 (longlora shift attention, packed attention, MoE and vision fixes), and unsloth support from model/model_utils/unsloth.py when requested. init_adapter at line 317 of model/adapter.py then branches: full tuning at line 38, freeze tuning at line 57, and _setup_lora_tuning at line 147 covering LoRA, DoRA, PiSSA, and LoftQ variants. The workflow finishes by instantiating CustomSeq2SeqTrainer at line 47 of train/sft/trainer.py with metrics from train/trainer_utils.py.

The serving half closes the loop. ChatModel at line 39 of chat/chat_model.py wraps three engines - hf, vLLM (VllmEngine at line 46 of chat/vllm_engine.py), and sglang - behind one astream_chat interface; api/app.py exposes it as an OpenAI-compatible server; and the LLaMA Board web UI’s webui/runner.py submits training jobs straight into the same run_exp entry, so GUI and CLI are one system. Evaluation through eval/evaluator.py scores MMLU-style benchmarks with the same template machinery.

Two registries make the 100-model claim hold up. The template registry in data/template.py is a plain dict called TEMPLATES at line 678, filled by register_template at line 681 and consulted by get_template_and_fix_tokenizer at line 819; the base Template class at line 41 carries specializations like Llama2Template at line 454 for the older Llama chat format, and ReasoningTemplate at line 524 with its Qwen38ReasoningTemplate subclass at line 593 for models that emit thinking traces before answers. Multimodal support follows the same shape in mm_plugin.py, a 3,502-line module whose BasePlugin at line 421 defines the default vision interface and whose per-family subclasses - Gemma3Plugin at line 876, InternVLPlugin at line 1180, KimiVLPlugin at line 1330, and LlavaPlugin at line 1429 - override how images and videos expand into placeholder tokens, how processor outputs are cached, and how the collator stitches visual features into the sequence. Adding a new model family usually means registering one template and one plugin instead of touching the trainer at all.

The alignment stages get their own trainers with minimal duplication. CustomDPOTrainer at line 44 of train/dpo/trainer.py extends the TRL DPOTrainer and overrides concatenated_forward at line 219 to route preference batches through the repo’s own collators and mm plugin, while CustomPPOTrainer at line 64 of train/ppo/trainer.py inherits from both PPOTrainer and Trainer to blend rollout generation with the standard optimization step. Cross-cutting behavior lands in callbacks rather than trainer edits: LogCallback at line 174 of train/callbacks.py appends each stage’s timing and loss to the trainer_log.jsonl you find in every output directory, PissaConvertCallback at line 132 swaps PiSSA adapters between their init and training representations, ReporterCallback at line 433 writes the training report when a run ends, and ModuleProfilerCallback at line 491 measures per-module memory so you can spot which layers are worth offloading or quantizing. When one node is not enough, run_exp checks ray_args.use_ray and re-enters itself through Ray, with the placement-group helpers in trainer_utils.py - get_placement_group, get_ray_head_node_ip, sort_placement_group_by_node_ip - pinning workers across the cluster, so the same YAML scales from a single GPU to a multi-node job without edits.

From Install to Fine-Tuned Model

The README’s zero-code loop:

uv run llamafactory-cli webui
llamafactory-cli train examples/train_lora/qwen3_lora_sft.yaml
llamafactory-cli chat examples/inference/qwen3_lora_sft.yaml
llamafactory-cli export examples/merge_lora/qwen3_lora_sft.yaml

Or programmatically, one dict instead of YAML:

from llamafactory.train.tuner import run_exp

run_exp(args={
    "stage": "sft",
    "model_name_or_path": "Qwen/Qwen3-8B",
    "template": "qwen3",
    "dataset": "alpaca_en_demo",
    "finetuning_type": "lora",
    "output_dir": "qwen3-lora-out",
})

Swap stage to dpo with a pairwise dataset and the same entry runs preference tuning; point infer_backend at vllm and the same chat model serves hundreds of concurrent requests.

Honest limits: the breadth comes with weight - the giant template, mm_plugin, and trainer_utils files are dense and occasionally duplicate logic across stage trainers, so tracing one behavior can mean reading three files. The WebUI covers the happy path well but exotic combinations still want the CLI. And because so much support is template registration plus small patches, per-model quirks sometimes surface only in that model’s issue tracker, not the docs.
entry.summary: A source tour of LLaMA-Factory, the unified fine-tuning factory: a 2686-line chat template registry, multimodal plugins, stage dispatch from pretraining to PPO, and a v1 engine rewrite.

entry.title: The Memory Core - Inside ggml-org/llama.cpp’s KV Cache Redesign

link.title: The Memory Core - Inside ggml-org/llama.cpp’s KV Cache Redesign

entry.content:
The most consequential project in local inference has quietly moved house - the repository now lives as ggml-org/llama.cpp - and while the logo stayed, the internals have been rebuilt around an abstraction that barely existed when this series first toured the codebase: a polymorphic memory layer. Where older versions wired a single KV cache directly into llama_context, the current master defines llama_memory_i in src/llama-memory.h and implements it five ways - the classic attention cache, a dual sliding-window cache, recurrent state cells, a hybrid of the two, and more - so that transformer models, Mamba-style models, and everything in between flow through one decode loop. This second tour of the project skips what we covered before and goes straight for the redesign: the memory interface, the find-slot machinery that decides whether your prompt fits, and the one-shot optimization retry that stands between you and an error.

As always in this series, what follows is an educational tour of published source code.

Overview: the public API feeds a decode loop that initializes batches, asks a polymorphic memory module for context, and processes ubatches through the graph; the KV cache anchors five implementations; failures trigger a one-shot optimization retry; the modular server drives it all from a task queue.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • src/llama.cpp is now just 621 lines of C API exports - the real engine lives in llama-context.cpp, 4,719 lines, whose decode at line 1821 is the single path every model takes.
  • llama_context::decode at line 1821 initializes the batch allocator at 1879, applies pending memory shifts at 1920, and enters a loop asking the memory module for a context via init_batch at 1925.
  • src/llama-batch.cpp, 1,493 lines, is the traffic splitter: llama_batch_allocr::init at line 28 validates input, then split_simple at 585, split_equal at 619, and split_seq at 790 carve one user batch into ubatches the graph can chew.
  • src/llama-memory.h is the new contract: init_batch at line 89, init_full at 95, init_update at 99, plus a seq_* family at 111-118 that gives every backend the same branching, copying, and position-shift vocabulary.
  • src/llama-kv-cache.cpp, 2,962 lines, is the reference implementation: prepare at line 771 walks ubatches, find_slot at 918 hunts for contiguous space, and apply_ubatch at 1117 commits the choice.
  • src/llama-kv-cache-iswa.cpp holds the SWA dual cache in 355 lines - a full cache for sinks and a sliding one for the rest - while llama-memory-hybrid.cpp, 283 lines, pairs attention and recurrent modules for Jamba-style architectures, and llama-memory-recurrent.cpp, 1,386 lines, keeps fixed-size state for Mamba-family models.
  • src/llama-sampler.cpp, 4,391 lines, chains token filters around one softmax at line 293: greedy at 1113, dist at 1405, top_k at 1525, top_p at 1725, min_p at 1888, typical at 2000, temp at 2110, xtc at 2422, grammar at 2831, and dry at 3645.
  • tools/server/server-queue.cpp, 621 lines, shows how far the server has modularized: post at line 28, deferred tasks at 76, and worker_loop at 163 - with a 6,313-line server-context.cpp, a 1,904-line server-task.cpp, and an MCP integration at server-mcp.cpp (799 lines) behind a main.cpp of just 5 lines.

Why You Need This

The polymorphic memory layer is the answer to a question this series keeps circling: how does one C++ codebase serve both a transformer and a state-space model without forking? The old answer was if-statements scattered through the context; the new answer is that llama_context holds a single llama_memory_i pointer and speaks only the interface - init_batch to start, seq_rm and seq_cp to edit, state_write at line 126 of the header to snapshot. When you run a Mamba model, the pointer points at llama-memory-recurrent.cpp; a hybrid Jamba architecture gets the 283-line coordinator; a Llama-family model gets the classic cache. Compare this with how vLLM bolted sliding-window support onto its paged allocator, or how ollama embeds an older llama.cpp and inherits whatever the snapshot had - reading the interface here shows what a clean second-architecture migration looks like when it is finished.

The find-slot machinery is worth its own visit because it is the heart of multi-sequence serving. find_slot at line 918 searches the cell grid for room for a ubatch - contiguity per sequence, headroom across the batch - and prepare at 771 runs it ahead of compute so failure is cheap. When preparation fails, decode’s status switch at 1930-1962 hits LLAMA_MEMORY_STATUS_FAILED_PREPARE and does exactly one thing: memory_update(true) at 1945, which shifts cache contents and optimizes fragmentation, then retries the same batch once - the debug line at 1946 says “retrying batch size after cache optimization,” and a second failure returns 1 at 1954. One retry, not a loop: the design accepts that a genuinely full context must fail loudly rather than thrash. Every LLM server reinvents this dance - llamafile sidesteps it with fixed allocations, TGI leans on its router’s queue - and seeing the minimal correct version in 30 lines is the best tutorial available.

Finally, the sampler file is a museum of decoding folklore, and the current layout teaches the chain-of-responsibility pattern with unusual clarity. Every filter - top_k, top_p, min_p, typical, temp, xtc, dry - is a tiny struct that mutates a token array in place, all funneling through the shared softmax at line 293, and the grammar sampler at 2831 simply zeroes out logits that the grammar forbids. The newest twist is backend sampling: decode opens a per-batch sampling transaction at 1974-1976 with llama_sampler_backend_begin, pushing the chain onto the GPU so the CPU never sees intermediate distributions - the same direction whisper.cpp took for its own hot loops. The sibling project comparison is not decorative: both live under the ggml umbrella, share ggml’s backend abstraction, and demonstrate how far a dependency-free C/C++ stack can stretch.

Detail: the decode loop wires batch splitting, memory preparation, graph building, and backend sampling; five memory backends share one sequence-operations vocabulary; the modular server queues tasks into the same C API.

The decode loop repays a full read. After the allocator initializes at 1879, decode counts outputs per sequence at 1853-1877 and rejects batches that exceed the backend-sampling output cap - a new constraint that did not exist when sampling lived on the CPU. The memory handoff at 1925 returns a llama_memory_context_ptr, a scoped object whose get_status() at 1930 tells the loop whether preparation succeeded; the one-shot optimize path lives at 1940-1955. Per ubatch, process_ubatch at line 1507 builds the graph via llama-graph.cpp (4,265 lines), computes, and on failure rolls back just the positions of that ubatch at 2004-2015 - an undo log in twelve lines. output_reorder at 2422 then untangles per-sequence outputs into batch order, and synchronize at 871 is the barrier callers hit before reading logits. The legacy llama_batch wrappers at 4601-4606 adapt the old public API onto llama_batch_ext, so years of downstream code keep compiling - a compatibility discipline worth copying in any long-lived library.

The KV cache itself is a small database, and the seq_* operations are its CRUD API. seq_rm at line 404 removes position ranges, seq_cp at 473 duplicates a sequence - the operation behind speculative decoding’s draft trees - seq_keep at 565 prunes everything else, and seq_add at 592 shifts positions, which is the mechanism behind context shifting when a conversation outgrows its window. prepare at 771 and find_slot at 918 enforce the invariants: cells for a ubatch must be contiguous per sequence, and get_can_shift at 1210 declares whether a backend can slide at all (recurrent state cannot; attention caches can). set_input_kq_mask at 1761 then writes the attention mask that encodes every one of those decisions into the graph - the last place where sequence bookkeeping becomes tensor data. The iswa variant at 355 lines runs two caches side by side because sliding-window layers and full-attention layers in the same model (Gemma-style interleaving) need different eviction horizons, and the hybrid coordinator delegates per layer type.

The server rewrite is the quiet headline of this tour. main.cpp is five lines; server.cpp holds 562; the actual behavior is spread across eighteen focused modules. server-queue.cpp posts tasks at line 28, defers continuation-style tasks at 76, and pops them when a slot frees at 90, while worker_loop at 163 drains the queue - a producer-consumer design that replaced the old monolithic loop. server-context.cpp (6,313 lines) owns inference slots and task execution, server-task.cpp (1,904 lines) defines the task types and result marshaling, server-mcp.cpp (799 lines) wires Model Context Protocol tool calling into completions, and the 5-line main is the reviewability payoff: a new contributor reads one module, not one monster. The same C API the CLI and bindings call is all the server uses, which keeps the library honest - if the server cannot do it through the public interface, users cannot either.

The model side stays the least changed. llama-model.cpp (3,985 lines) and the loader build tensor graphs per architecture at load time, llama-grammar.cpp (1,530 lines) implements the GBNF engine that the grammar sampler consults, and the whole stack sits on ggml’s backend abstraction - CPU, CUDA, Metal, Vulkan, SYCL - so the memory layer above never learns which hardware is underneath. That layering, interface over implementation over hardware, is the durable lesson of this codebase: the parts that were refactored (memory, server) are exactly the parts that had leaked across layers, and the parts left alone were already clean.

From Install to a Cached Sequence

Building and driving the server still takes three commands (abridged):

cmake -B build && cmake --build build --config Release -j
./build/bin/llama-server -m models/qwen2.5-7b-q4_k_m.gguf --ctx-size 8192 --port 8080
curl http://localhost:8080/v1/chat/completions -d '{"messages":[{"role":"user","content":"hi"}]}'
# observe the cache at work:
curl http://localhost:8080/props | head   # default_generation_settings, slots

Prompt caching is automatic: a follow-up request sharing the conversation prefix finds its cells via find_slot and computes only the new tokens - watch the timings field report n_prompt_tokens_processed shrinking to single digits.

Honest limits: the memory redesign is C++17 through and through, and the interface’s power comes with pointer juggling that demands care from embedders; the one-shot optimization retry means pathological fragmentation patterns can still fail a batch that a second retry would fit; recurrent memory keeps fixed-size state, so long-context claims for Mamba-family models depend on that state size, not on cache eviction; backend sampling caps outputs per sequence (enforced at decode 1853-1877), which unusual batch shapes can hit unexpectedly; the server’s 6,313-line context module is a lot of state in one file despite the modularization; and the org move to ggml-org means old clone URLs redirect - pin your remotes and your known_hosts.
entry.summary: A second source tour of llama.cpp, now under ggml-org: the unified llama_memory interface, the KV cache find-slot machinery, SWA and hybrid and recurrent backends, batch splitting, the decode retry loop, and the modularized task-queue server.

entry.title: The Ruler Every LLM Paper Trusts - Inside EleutherAI/lm-evaluation-harness

link.title: The Ruler Every LLM Paper Trusts - Inside EleutherAI/lm-evaluation-harness

entry.content:
Every benchmark number you have seen attached to an open model - MMLU, HellaSwag, GSM8K, ARC, TruthfulQA - has a decent chance of having been produced by this repository. EleutherAI’s Language Model Evaluation Harness is the framework behind the Open LLM Leaderboard and hundreds of papers, and its power comes from an architecture that treats evaluation as data: every task is a YAML file describing prompts, document formats, and metrics, and the framework’s job is to turn any language model into a scoring function against those files. Release 0.4.14 under the MIT license ships with 221 task directories under lm_eval/tasks, each holding configs that expand into hundreds of benchmark subtasks and variants.

What makes the source worth reading is that it is a masterclass in interface design under constraint. The whole system communicates through two verbs - loglikelihood and generate_until - so anything that can answer those two requests becomes an evaluable model, from a Hugging Face checkpoint to a vLLM engine to a commercial API to a llama.cpp GGUF file. Around that spine sits a task system powerful enough to encode fewshot selection, answer extraction, and metric aggregation as declarative config, plus a plugin registry that keeps 30 model backends from tangling the core. As always in this series, what follows is an educational tour of published source code.

Overview: the CLI drives the evaluator, which pulls tasks from the manager and requests from the model abstraction; answers flow through filters into aggregation and result logging.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • lm_eval/_cli/run.py is the 518-line entry that parses CLI flags into a simple_evaluate call.
  • lm_eval/evaluator.py holds the two public functions: simple_evaluate at line 55 and the core evaluate loop at line 429 of its 714 lines.
  • lm_eval/tasks/manager.py defines TaskManager at line 37, the indexer that turns task names into config-loaded classes.
  • lm_eval/api/task.py is the 1808-line heart: Task at line 64, ConfigurableTask at line 618.
  • lm_eval/api/model.py declares the LM interface at line 25 with TemplateLM at line 356 and CachingLM at line 275.
  • lm_eval/models/huggingface.py is the reference backend, HFLM at line 62 of 1782 lines.
  • lm_eval/api/filter.py pairs the Filter contract at line 8 with FilterEnsemble at line 34, fed by regex extractors in filters/extraction.py.
  • lm_eval/loggers/evaluation_tracker.py persists everything through EvaluationTracker at line 123.

Why You Need This

If you have followed the fine-tuning tours here - LLaMA-Factory, axolotl, unsloth - you have watched the training side of the loop. The harness is the other half: the tool that tells you whether a model got better. Reading it teaches you what benchmark numbers actually measure, because every step that could silently change a score is explicit: which prompt template was used, how many fewshot examples were sampled and by what rule, how the raw generation was cut down to an answer, and which aggregation produced the table cell. Reproducibility is not a slogan here; it is enforced by config files checked into the repo.

The backend abstraction is the lesson most applicable elsewhere. Anything implementing loglikelihood and generate_until plugs in - and the catalog shows the range: HFLM for transformers checkpoints with quantization support, VLLM for batched inference throughput, TemplateAPI for OpenAI-compatible endpoints, Megatron for very large models, plus GGUF, ONNX, and Neuron variants. The same interface idea powers ctranslate2 and onnxruntime in serving, and seeing it applied to evaluation makes a strong argument for tiny, honest interfaces over framework lock-in.

The task system deserves study if you ever design datasets or leaderboards. ConfigurableTask turns a YAML file into prompt construction, target extraction, and metric selection, while the filter ensemble composes regex extraction, whitespace trimming, and majority-vote selection into the answer stage. The metric library covers everything from exact match and F1 to BLEU, chrF, perplexity, and bits-per-byte, with aggregation declared per task so nothing is hard-coded. Once you have seen how much behavior fits in declarative config, you will never hard-code an eval script again.

Detailed view: CLI entry, the evaluation core, the task API with metrics and samplers, the backend family registered against the LM interface, task definition loading, filters, and logging with caching.

The main flow starts at simple_evaluate at line 55 of evaluator.py, which resolves the model through get_model at line 613 of api/registry.py, builds the task list through a TaskManager constructed in tasks/manager.py, applies decontamination and limits, and then hands everything to evaluate at line 429 - the loop that batches requests per task, sorts them across tasks for throughput, calls the model, and routes outputs through filters and aggregation. The supporting math lands in evaluator_utils.py: get_sample_size at line 49, the aggregation accumulator at line 99, group-aware rollups through aggregate_groups at line 301, and result shaping in _process_results at line 375 of its 540 lines.
