The registry is the hinge of the whole design. Registry at line 270 of api/registry.py is a generic plugin container fed by load_plugins at line 189 and import_plugins at line 246; register_model at line 587 lets any backend class join the catalog by name, DEFAULT_METRIC_REGISTRY at line 571 maps task output types to default metrics, and get_model at line 613 is the single factory call the evaluator makes. This is why the models directory can hold thirty backends - anthropic, openai_completions, textsynth, sglang, trtllm, neuron, watsonx - without the core importing any of them.

The breadth of that directory repays a skim. HFMultimodalLM at line 30 of models/hf_vlms.py extends HFLM across its 750 lines for vision-language checkpoints; MambaLMWrapper at line 10 of models/mamba_lm.py shows a state-space model joining the club through the same base class in just 164 lines; GGUFLM at line 24 of models/gguf.py implements the LM interface directly to talk to llama.cpp; and TRTLLM at line 37 of models/trtllm_causallms.py covers TensorRT-LLM deployments in 631 lines. Even audio generation gets a slot through hf_audiolm.py, and the thinness of the smaller wrappers is the point - the easier a backend is to write, the better the interface is doing its job.

Every backend implements the same small interface from api/model.py: LM at line 25 declares loglikelihood, loglikelihood_rolling, and generate_until; TemplateLM at line 356 implements the shared tokenization glue for models that expose token access; CachingLM at line 275 wraps any backend with a sqlite cache keyed by hash_args at line 255, so repeated runs replay identical requests for free. The reference implementation, HFLM at line 62 of models/huggingface.py, handles device placement, batching, PEFT adapters, and quantized checkpoints across its 1782 lines; VLLM at line 59 of models/vllm_causallms.py swaps throughput into the same contract; and TemplateAPI at line 105 of models/api_models.py does the same for remote endpoints, with shared helpers like handle_stop_sequences at line 641 of models/utils.py keeping behavior aligned.

The task layer is where YAML becomes evaluation. TaskManager at line 37 indexes every task config, tasks/_yaml_loader.py loads them with include-resolution and safe function imports through load_yaml at line 164, and tasks/_factory.py builds concrete tasks through TaskFactory at line 25. The resulting ConfigurableTask at line 618 of api/task.py is an engine of over a thousand lines that constructs fewshot contexts through ContextSampler at line 17 of api/samplers.py (with FirstNSampler, BalancedSampler at line 117, and ManualSampler variants), builds Instance requests from api/instance.py, scores outputs with the metric functions in api/metrics.py - mean at line 35, perplexity at line 47, f1_score at line 62, bleu at line 102 - and specializes into MultipleChoiceTask at line 1688 and PerplexityTask at line 1735 for the two classic evaluation shapes. Groups compose tasks hierarchically through Group at line 34 of api/group.py and ConfigurableGroup at line 346.

Answer extraction gets its own layer because raw generations rarely match gold strings directly. Filter at line 8 of api/filter.py is the contract and FilterEnsemble at line 34 chains several; filters/extraction.py provides RegexFilter at line 16, a POS-aware filter at line 66, WhitespaceFilter at line 110, and MultiChoiceRegexFilter at line 123 for multiple-choice formats, while filters/selection.py implements majority voting over sampled generations. Results finally flow through the logging stack: GeneralConfigTracker at line 38 and EvaluationTracker at line 123 of loggers/evaluation_tracker.py write samples, configs, and tables to disk or the Hub, loggers/wandb_logger.py streams the same to experiment dashboards, and the 88 lines of caching/cache.py back the request cache that makes reruns nearly instant. Even discovery is a first-class feature - lm_eval/_cli/ls.py powers lm-eval ls tasks and ls models against the same index the runner consumes.

From Install to a Benchmark Table

Install with the backends you need, then evaluate:

pip install "lm_eval[hf,vllm]"
lm_eval --model hf \
    --model_args pretrained=EleutherAI/pythia-1.4b \
    --tasks hellaswag,arc_easy \
    --device cuda:0 --batch_size 8

The same run from Python:

import lm_eval

results = lm_eval.simple_evaluate(
    model="hf",
    model_args="pretrained=EleutherAI/pythia-1.4b",
    tasks=["hellaswag", "arc_easy"],
    num_fewshot=0,
)
print(results["results"])

Both paths return per-task metric tables plus samples you can inspect, and the tracker writes them to JSON for later comparison.

Honest limits: benchmark scores are proxies, and the harness makes prompt and extraction choices visible but cannot make them neutral; a few backend integrations lag the latest upstream releases; and running 221 task groups naively costs real money and compute, so sane usage starts with limit and a hand-picked task list. The value of the source is that none of these limits are hidden - every choice is a line you can read.
entry.summary: A source tour of the EleutherAI evaluation harness: one YAML-driven ConfigurableTask format, a plugin registry of model backends from Hugging Face to vLLM to llama.cpp, fewshot samplers, regex answer filters, and the aggregation machinery behind benchmark tables.

entry.title: Five Calls from Data to Fine-Tuned Model - Inside OptimalScale/LMFlow

link.title: Five Calls from Data to Fine-Tuned Model - Inside OptimalScale/LMFlow

entry.content:
Every fine-tuning toolbox has a philosophy. axolotl bets on YAML, LLaMA-Factory on a hundred CLI flags, unsloth on monkey-patching, and ms-swift on mixin-composed trainers. LMFlow, from the Statistics and Machine Learning Research Group at HKUST, bets on something subtler: a small set of stable abstractions - model, dataset, and a family of aligner and tuner objects - with everything else pushed to the edges. The result is Apache-2.0 licensed, version 1.1.0, and notable for shipping its own research: RAFT (Reward rAnked FineTuning) and LISA (Layerwise Importance Sampling) were born here, the latter letting a 7B model train in 24GB without offloading. A major rewrite in July 2025 moved the stack onto Accelerate with optional extras for vLLM, SGLang, and TRL, and the project took the Best Demo Paper Award at NAACL 2024 along the way.

As always in this series, what follows is an educational tour of published source code.

Overview: examples and dataclass arguments on the left, the dataset and conversation-template layer, the model abstraction, the tuner-aligner-inferencer stages, and the optimizer and protocol libraries underneath.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • examples/finetune.py is the whole driver story in 60 lines: main at line 32 parses three argument dataclasses, requests a Finetuner from the package’s stage dispatcher, wraps a Dataset, loads a model through AutoModel, and calls tune at line 56.
  • lmflow/args.py is the 1418-line argument universe: OptimizerNames at line 34, ModelArguments at 58, DatasetArguments at 418, FinetunerArguments at 626, InferencerArguments at 853, and AutoArguments at 1408, which maps a stage name to its argument class.
  • lmflow/datasets/dataset.py defines Dataset at line 53, a backend-wrapping container with from_dict at 150, map at 309, sample at 397, train_test_split at 427, and sanity_check at 483.
  • lmflow/models/auto_model.py is a 22-line dispatch: AutoModel at line 10 routes arch_type “decoder_only” to HFDecoderModel and “text_regression” to HFTextRegressionModel.
  • lmflow/models/hf_model_mixin.py holds HFModelMixin at line 43, 608 lines of private preparation - __prepare_quant_config at 203, __prepare_peft_config at 248, __prepare_model_for_training at 323, activate_model_for_inference at 518.
  • lmflow/models/hf_decoder_model.py defines HFDecoderModel at line 57 with tokenize at 81, inference at 313, dedicated __vllm_inference at 430 and __sglang_inference at 456 branches, and merge_lora_weights at 577.
  • lmflow/optim/utils.py provides create_customized_optimizer at line 10, which synthesizes a trainer subclass whose get_optimizer_cls_and_kwargs at line 13 selects from a 22-module optimizer zoo including Muon at line 41 of muon.py and SophiaG at line 7 of sophia.py.
  • lmflow/utils/protocol.py defines DataProto at line 257, a 1067-line tensor-container module with union at 688, make_iterator at 707, and chunk at 762 - the currency for handing generation results into the next alignment round.

Why You Need This

The layering is the draw. LMFlow’s BaseModel at line 5 of lmflow/models/base_model.py is six lines long, and the HF-specific implementation arrives as a mixin you compose rather than a hierarchy you inherit: HFDecoderModel at line 57 of hf_decoder_model.py combines DecoderModel, HFModelMixin, and a six-line Tunable interface from lmflow/models/interfaces/tunable.py. If you have read trl’s trainer-centric design or ms-swift’s factory-composed trainers, this is a third point in the design space - closer to a library than a framework, which is exactly why its aligners are so easy to read.

The alignment catalog is the second reason. DPO, DPOv2, iterative DPO, RAFT, and reward-model tuning each live in their own stage class, and LMFlow does not pretend one trainer fits all: the RAFT aligner carries its own vendored 3786-line Trainer copy (RaftTrainer at line 209 of raft_trainer.py) because the algorithm predates transformers 4.35, while DPOv2 rides TRL’s DPOTrainer with a custom dpo_loss at line 102 of dpov2_trainer.py and a reward-length-penalty pairing scheme. Iterative DPO loops target-model sampling, reward scoring, and preference-pair construction in a single align method. Compare this with OpenRLHF’s single-controller PPO or axolotl’s GRPO trainers, and the algorithm-as-a-class style becomes very legible - each aligner’s align() is a readable script for one research idea.

Third, the edges of the package are full of genuinely useful tools you rarely see in one place: LISA’s DynamicLayerActivationCallback at line 8 of lisa_trainer.py is 66 lines that freeze and unfreeze layer ranges on a schedule; the optimizer zoo ships 22 implementations from AdaBelief to LARS to Muon with a README benchmark table; the Evaluator at line 46 of evaluator.py implements accuracy and perplexity paths over Accelerate and DeepSpeed; and the inferencer family includes speculative decoding (SpeculativeInferencer at line 318) and a tool-calling variant whose code_exec at line 628 runs model-emitted Python. For benchmarking the trained result, the README itself points to lm-evaluation-harness, which we toured earlier, and for LoRA internals you can pair this tour with peft and unsloth.

Detailed view: the entry dispatcher with extras-conditional registration, data and template machinery, the model abstraction, tuning with LISA, the alignment algorithm family with its vendored trainer, inference backends, and the optimizer zoo.

A run begins in examples/finetune.py: main at line 32 resolves the stage-specific argument class through AutoArguments at line 1408 of lmflow/args.py, then lets HfArgumentParser fill ModelArguments at 58, DatasetArguments at 418, and the stage arguments in one pass. The dispatcher that turns the name “finetuner” into a Finetuner object is deliberately boring - a name-to-class registry - but its registration block is where the extras system lives: the SGLang and vLLM inferencers join the registry only when their packages import (the availability probes are is_vllm_available at line 60 and is_sglang_available at line 64 of lmflow/utils/versioning.py), the DPO aligners require TRL, and the RAFT aligner is registered only below transformers 4.35, matching the vendored trainer it depends on. The same pattern drives the model side: AutoModel.get_model at line 12 of auto_model.py reads arch_type and returns HFDecoderModel or HFTextRegressionModel, nothing else.

The model layer is a study in mixin composition. HFModelMixin at line 43 of lmflow/models/hf_model_mixin.py runs a chain of private preparers - __prepare_tokenizer at 94, __prepare_dtype at 133, __prepare_model_config at 159, __prepare_quant_config at 203 for the QLoRA paths, __prepare_peft_config at 248, then __prepare_model_for_training at 323 or __prepare_model_for_inference at 386 depending on the phase - and exposes activate_model_for_inference at 518 and deactivate_model_for_inference at 556 so stages can borrow the model between rounds. HFDecoderModel at line 57 of lmflow/models/hf_decoder_model.py adds the tokenizer-adjacent work: tokenize at 81, encode at 234, decode at 271, inference at 313 with __vllm_inference at 430 and __sglang_inference at 456 as dedicated backend branches, prepare_inputs_for_inference at 481, and checkpoint utilities merge_lora_weights at 577 and get_peft_without_qlora at 590. The regression sibling at line 45 of lmflow/models/hf_text_regression_model.py is the 424-line reward-model class, and the multimodal path pairs CustomAutoVision2SeqModel at line 31 of lmflow/models/vision2seq_model.py with a 294-line CLIP wrapper in lmflow/models/vision_encoder/clip_encoder.py.

Data flows through one container class. Dataset at line 53 of lmflow/datasets/dataset.py wraps a Hugging Face or JSON backend behind from_dict at 150, create_from_dict at 235, map at 309, sample at 397, and train_test_split at 427, with sanity_check at 483 catching malformed instances before they reach the trainer; the multimodal sibling in lmflow/datasets/multi_modal_dataset.py adds 291 lines for image-text corpora. Tokenization lives in lmflow/tokenization/hf_decoder_model.py - blocking at 19, tokenize_function at 57, and conversation_tokenize_function at 111, which consults the template layer. That layer, lmflow/utils/conversation_template/base.py, models a chat format as TemplateComponent lists (line 18) built by formatters (StringFormatter at 115), with ConversationTemplate at 154 providing encode_conversation at 180 and post_process_pairs at 299, and ConversationTemplateForTool at 403 adding _handle_tools at 542 for function-calling formats. Thirteen per-family modules subclass it - qwen.py at 414 lines, deepseek.py at 244, llama.py with Llama2ConversationTemplate at line 16 - and the Finetuner consumes the result through group_text at line 131 of finetuner.py, which packs tokenized sequences to model_max_length exactly the way axolotl’s packing and ms-swift’s padding-free batches do.

The alignment family is where the research lives. Finetuner at line 40 (its tune method at 222) handles full, LoRA, and QLoRA runs, and LISA plugs in as DynamicLayerActivationCallback at line 8 of lisa_trainer.py: freeze_all_layers at 43, on_step_begin at 49, and switch_active_layers at 54 rotate a budget of active layers on an interval - the layerwise importance sampling from the group’s own paper, and a cousin of the memory tricks in deepspeed and colossalai. DPOAligner at line 72 of dpo_aligner.py pairs a policy and reference through TRL, while DPOv2Aligner at line 30 of dpov2_aligner.py goes deeper: convert_to_paired_dataset at 143, _calc_reward_with_length_penalty at 198, and sampling_paired_idx_from_rewards at 210 build chosen/rejected pairs by reward, with MemorySafeDPOv2Aligner at 273 wrapping the same logic in a subprocess. IterativeDPOAligner at line 29 of iterative_dpo_aligner.py orchestrates rounds - _align_single_iteration at 66 calls _do_target_model_inference at 120, then _do_reward_model_inference at 185, then _do_single_dpo_align at 210, passing DataProto batches between steps. RaftAligner at line 34 of raft_aligner.py takes the other road: _get_batch_dataset_top at 257 ranks samples by reward-model score, keeps the top fraction, and simply fine-tunes on winners via align at 545 - no preference pairs at all - which is why it carries the vendored RaftTrainer at line 209 of raft_trainer.py, 3786 lines with train at 1517 and its own get_optimizer_cls_and_kwargs at 1059. The reward models themselves are trained and served by RewardModelTuner at line 16 of rm_tuner.py and RewardModelInferencer at line 41, both sitting on the regression model class.

Serving and evaluation close the loop. Inferencer at line 45 (with create_dataloader at 99, inference at 128, and streaming at 270) is the HF-backend default; SpeculativeInferencer at 318 implements draft-then-verify decoding with autoregressive_sampling at 422; ToolInferencer at 565 answers with tool calls and executes Python via code_exec at 628. VLLMInferencer at line 37 of vllm_inferencer.py adds batch throughput with _parse_args_to_sampling_params at 51 and a memory-safe subprocess variant at 122, returning results as DataProto at line 257 of lmflow/utils/protocol.py - a tensor-dict container whose chunk at 762, concat at 815, repeat at 869, and sample_level_repeat at 952 make it a smaller cousin of the data movement in OpenRLHF’s experience buffers. Evaluator at line 46 of evaluator.py finishes the story with evaluate at 142 dispatching to _evaluate_acc_with_accelerate at 179, _evaluate_acc_with_deepspeed at 287, _evaluate_ppl at 391, and _evaluate_nll at 440, using answer_extraction at line 155 of lmflow/utils/data_utils.py to grade free-form outputs.

From Install to a Fine-Tuned Model

The README’s recommended setup targets Linux and pins version 1.0.0 or later:

git clone -b v1.0.0 https://github.com/OptimalScale/LMFlow.git
cd LMFlow
conda create -n lmflow python=3.9 -y
conda activate lmflow
conda install mpi4py
pip install -e .

Then a LoRA run on Llama-2-7B with a conversation template:

cd data && ./download.sh alpaca && cd -
bash ./scripts/run_finetune_with_lora.sh \
  --model_name_or_path meta-llama/Llama-2-7b-hf \
  --dataset_path data/alpaca/train_conversation \
  --conversation_template llama2 \
  --output_model_path output_models/finetuned_llama2_7b_lora

Swap the script for run_finetune_with_lisa.sh and add –lisa_activated_layers 1 –lisa_interval_steps 20 to train with LISA’s rotating layer budget, or run_finetune_with_custom_optim.sh to pick any of the 22 optimizers. The Python API is the five-call sequence from examples/finetune.py - argument classes, dispatcher, Dataset, AutoModel, tune - and extras like pip install -e ".[vllm,trl]" unlock the vLLM-backed iterative DPO loop.

Honest limits: the README states the package is fully tested on Ubuntu and only partially elsewhere; the RAFT aligner is pinned to transformers below 4.35 because of its vendored trainer; vLLM and SGLang must live in separate environments due to CUDA conflicts; and WandB reporting is on by default until you pass –report_to none. The abstraction seams are visible, though - every algorithm is one aligner class you can read top to bottom, which is rarer than it should be.
entry.summary: A source tour of LMFlow: dataclass arguments, model mixins, DPO, DPOv2, RAFT and iterative-DPO aligners, LISA layer freezing, a 22-optimizer zoo, and speculative decoding.

entry.title: One Framework from Tuning to Deployment - Inside modelscope/ms-swift

link.title: One Framework from Tuning to Deployment - Inside modelscope/ms-swift

entry.content:
ModelScope’s ms-swift has a scope that makes most fine-tuning frameworks look modest: supervised tuning, preference optimization, GRPO-style reinforcement learning, knowledge distillation, multimodal training, Megatron-backed large runs, quantized export, and deployment, all in one package. The current development line, version 4.7.0.dev0 under an Apache-2.0 license, organizes that breadth with an unusual pattern - rather than one monolithic trainer, a factory composes small mixin classes into exactly the trainer a task needs, and the same composition style repeats in the adapter system, the template engine, and the inference layer. The result is a codebase where the fastest way to understand any feature is to find its mixin.

It is also one of the few frameworks where the ModelScale ecosystem assumptions pay off visibly: datasets load straight from the Hub, templates read metadata registered alongside the models, and the CLI treats training, rollout sampling, evaluation, and deployment as sibling subcommands of one binary. For anyone who has outgrown single-purpose scripts, this is a case study in layering without sprawl. As always in this series, what follows is an educational tour of published source code.

Overview: the CLI parses argument trees and dispatches to a trainer factory; mixins compose into SFT and RLHF trainers; templates and datasets feed training while adapters reshape models and inference engines close the loop.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • swift/cli/main.py is the 106-line router: parse_yaml_args at line 38 merges YAML config files with command-line flags, and cli_main at line 86 maps subcommands to entry modules.
  • swift/arguments/sft_args.py holds the 434-line SFT argument tree; the RLHF counterpart in swift/arguments/rlhf_args.py runs 773 lines.
  • swift/trainers/trainer_factory.py defines TrainerFactory at line 12, the class-composition switch for every training stage.
  • swift/trainers/mixin.py is the shared behavior core, SwiftMixin at line 70 of 1495 lines with DataLoaderMixin at line 1352.
  • swift/rlhf_trainers/grpo_trainer.py is the largest single file in the package: GRPOTrainer at line 84 of 2623 lines.
  • swift/template/base.py defines Template at line 43, the 2502-line encoder that turns conversations into tensors.
  • swift/tuners/base.py exposes SwiftModel at line 31 and the Swift facade at line 702 for ten adapter types.
  • swift/infer_engine/vllm_engine.py wraps vLLM in VllmEngine at line 121 of 968 lines.

Why You Need This

The mixin-composition pattern is the main draw. Instead of inheriting a fixed hierarchy, TrainerFactory at line 12 of trainer_factory.py picks a TRL or HF trainer class, mixes in SwiftMixin for dataset handling, adapter mounting, and loss scaling, and hands back a trainer whose behavior is assembled from parts. If you have ever wished the Hugging Face Trainer were easier to customize, or wondered how TRL-style trainers get extended without forking them, this file is a clean answer - and it contrasts nicely with the config-driven dispatch of LLaMA-Factory and the patch-first strategy of unsloth.

The template engine is the second reason. Multimodal chat models need text, images, videos, and audio interleaved into one token sequence with loss masks, and ms-swift’s Template class at line 43 of template/base.py does that encoding generically - 2502 lines covering grounding boxes, tool calls, thinking modes, and per-model quirks through a metadata system. Combined with the dataset layer’s media handling, it is one of the most complete public implementations of what “apply_chat_template” actually has to do for real model families. The RLHF stack rides on it: GRPO with async vLLM rollouts, DPO and its CPO/ORPO/KTO relatives, PPO, and Generative Knowledge Distillation all share the same data plumbing, an approach you can compare directly with OpenRLHF’s single-controller design or axolotl’s GRPO trainers.

Finally, the adapter zoo is worth the visit on its own. SwiftModel at line 31 of tuners/base.py wraps any model so that LoRA, LLaMA-Pro’s layer expansion, Restuning’s bottleneck adapters, ReFT representation edits, NEFTune noise, and more attach through one interface - a broader catalog than peft alone ships, built on top of it where possible. The Megatron subpackage extends the same argument surface to very large models the way deepspeed or colossalai users would expect, and the inference engines - vLLM, LMDeploy, SGLang, plain PyTorch - all speak one protocol module, which makes the train-to-deploy loop of lm-evaluation-harness-style benchmarking trivial to attach.

Detailed view: CLI routing, argument families, the training core with its mixin, the RLHF trainer family with rollout machinery, templates and datasets, adapters, inference engines, and the model registry.

A run begins in cli/main.py, where cli_main at line 86 resolves the subcommand - the individual entries are tiny, with cli/sft.py at 20 lines and cli/rlhf.py at 7 - and torchrun relaunching is handled by use_torchrun at line 30. Arguments layer into families: SFTArgs in arguments/sft_args.py embeds the tuner arguments of arguments/tuner_args.py, while the RLHF tree in arguments/rlhf_args.py adds rollout, reward, and vLLM server sections. Everything lands in TrainerFactory at line 12 of trainers/trainer_factory.py, a 75-line file that decides which composed trainer class to build from the stage, train type, and backend flags.

The mixin is where the real work hides. SwiftMixin at line 70 of trainers/mixin.py owns the shared lifecycle - loading model and template, mounting adapters, preparing losses - while DataLoaderMixin at line 1352 builds the batch streams, including the packing path from dataset/packing.py. Trainer construction goes through trainers/trainer.py, whose 74 lines define the SFT and CPT trainer classes on top of the mixin, and upstream Trainer behavior is adjusted by trainers/patcher.py plus the helpers in trainers/utils.py. Dataset loading flows through dataset/loader.py, a 421-line loader that mixes registered datasets with per-dataset sampling weights, backed by the registry in dataset/register.py and metadata in dataset_meta.py. The terse dataset strings the CLI accepts are parsed by DatasetSyntax at line 56 of dataset/dataset_syntax.py, whose docstring spells out the grammar - hf/ms::dataset_id or path:subset1/subset2#sample_count - so the #500 suffix in the quickstart below literally means “take 500 rows of this corpus”. The registry side is two functions: register_dataset at line 24 of dataset/register.py files DatasetMeta records declared in dataset/dataset_meta.py (DatasetMeta at line 174, SubsetDataset at line 27), and get_dataset_list at line 14 resolves names to metadata - the same three-part registry-plus-syntax pattern that templates and models use.

The RLHF family shows the same composition at its most elaborate. GRPOTrainer at line 84 of rlhf_trainers/grpo_trainer.py - 2623 lines, the package’s biggest file - composes RolloutTrainerMixin, SwiftMixin, and TRL’s GRPO trainer. RolloutTrainerMixin at line 91 of rlhf_trainers/rollout_mixin.py is the 1853-line bridge between training and generation: AsyncGenerateCallback at line 66 overlaps sampling with optimization, SyncRefModelCallback at line 78 keeps a remote reference model fresh, and the mixin drives either an in-process vLLM engine or the external server client at rlhf_trainers/vllm_client.py, 550 lines that manage weight sync and cache reset over HTTP. The preference branch centers on rlhf_trainers/dpo_trainer.py at 519 lines (with CPO and ORPO variants nearby), PPO at rlhf_trainers/ppo_trainer.py, KTO at 130 lines, reward-model training in reward_trainer.py, and the distillation pair of gkd_trainer.py and gkd_loss.py - Generative Knowledge Distillation where the student learns from the teacher’s own generations.

Templates deserve their own paragraph because they carry the multimodal weight. TemplateMeta in template/template_meta.py declares a model family’s system prompt, stop words, and special tokens; register_template at line 16 of template/register.py files hundreds of these registrations, and get_template at line 55 resolves one from model metadata read out of the checkpoint directory. The base Template at line 43 of template/base.py then encodes messages - including vision and audio inputs through template/vision_utils.py - into input ids, labels, and loss masks that the trainers consume directly. The adapter side mirrors this registry style: SwiftModel at line 31 and Swift at line 702 of tuners/base.py activate LoRA from tuners/lora.py with its custom tuners/lora_layers.py, LLaMA-Pro block expansion from tuners/llamapro.py, and the rest from sibling modules.

Serving and the model registry close the loop. InferEngine at line 22 of infer_engine/infer_engine.py defines the common request surface; VllmEngine at line 121 of infer_engine/vllm_engine.py implements it for vLLM (with compatibility patches like _patch_vllm_dp_coordinator_timeout at line 54), while transformers_engine.py, lmdeploy_engine.py, and sglang_engine.py cover the other backends, all speaking the request shapes in infer_engine/protocol.py. Under everything sits the model registry: model_arch.py at 926 lines maps architectures to module names, register.py at 689 lines files per-model metadata and loading adjustments, and patcher.py at 726 lines carries the per-family fixes. Model names themselves live as enum members in model/constant.py, 313 lines where LLMModelType at line 6, MLLMModelType at line 144, and reward-model and BERT entries at lines 130 and 136 merge into a ModelType union at line 295 - the same three-part pattern the template and dataset systems use, which is the codebase’s real signature.

From Install to a Fine-Tuned Model

The README’s 13GB one-GPU run:

pip install ms-swift
CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0 swift sft \
    --model Qwen/Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 \
    --tuner_type lora \
    --dataset AI-ModelScope/alpaca-gpt4-data-zh#500 \
              AI-ModelScope/alpaca-gpt4-data-en#500 \
    --lora_rank 8 --lora_alpha 32 \
    --target_modules all-linear \
    --max_length 2048 --output_dir output

Inference and export use the same style:

CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0 swift infer --adapters output/checkpoint-xx --infer_backend vllm
CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0 swift export --adapters output/checkpoint-xx --merge_lora true

The Python API mirrors it: swift.llm exposes the same argument objects, so a script can construct TrainArguments and call the trainer factory directly.

Honest limits: the argument surface is huge and moves fast between minor versions, so blog posts and tutorials age quickly; Megatron and RLHF paths assume multi-GPU comfort; and the mixin composition, while elegant, means a debugger steps through more classes than a monolithic trainer would. The payoff is breadth with visible seams - almost everything is one registry entry away from view.
entry.summary: A source tour of ms-swift: a TrainerFactory that composes mixins into trainers, a 2500-line Template engine for chat and multimodal encoding, ten adapter types behind SwiftModel, RLHF trainers with vLLM rollouts, and inference engines that share one protocol.

entry.title: The Landlord of Your VRAM - The Scheduler Inside ollama/ollama

link.title: The Landlord of Your VRAM - The Scheduler Inside ollama/ollama

entry.content:
Run two models back to back in Ollama and something peculiar happens: the second model loads in about the time a browser tab takes to appear, and when you return to the first, it is warm again. That feeling of infinite memory is the work of one Go file - server/sched.go, 1,851 lines - which decides what stays resident, what gets evicted, which GPU group receives each model, and how long a loaded runner lingers before being shown the door. This is our third visit to the ollama repository; the first two tours covered the server surface and the manifest machinery, so this time we go where the real memory management lives: the scheduler that treats your VRAM like a landlord treats apartments, with pre-flight fit checks, eviction notices, and a very precise definition of how long a tenant may stay after its last request.

As always in this series, what follows is an educational tour of published source code.

Overview: HTTP handlers schedule requests through getRunner; the pending loop reuses, evicts, or loads; each load predicts VRAM, selects a GPU placement, and pre-flights the fit; completions release reference counts into keep-alive timers; device discovery refreshes the candidate list.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • server/routes.go, 3,653 lines, is the API surface: GenerateHandler at line 308 and EmbedHandler at 1082 both end at the same scheduler call, while PullHandler at 1480 and ShowHandler at 1745 handle the manifest side of the house.
  • server/sched.go defines LlmRequest at line 31 and the Scheduler at 62, initialized by InitScheduler at 131 with a loaded map keyed by schedulerModelKey at 152 so identical requests share one runner.
  • getRunner at line 218 is the entry every request passes: it floors the context at 4 tokens (219-221), raises it to 2,048 for vision models at 223-226, resolves the context-shift flag at 228-231, and either reuses a live runner at 250 or enqueues into pendingReqCh at 254 - returning ErrMaxQueue when the channel is full.
  • The pending loop, processPending at line 274, is the landlord: it blocks the queue while it works, consults envconfig.MaxRunners at 275, reuses via needsReload checks at 305-313, and otherwise refreshes the GPU list at 320-326 before attempting a load.
  • Scheduler.load at line 545 does the heavy lifting: it loads GGUF metadata at 576, asks the llm package to PredictServerVRAM at 585, and calls selectLlamaServerPlacement at 586 to choose which devices will host the model.
  • The placement engine selectLlamaServerPlacement at line 1014 walks candidate groups - bestSingleGPUFit at 1102, multi-GPU spreads, or main-GPU preferences at 1081 - scoring each by available memory after the load.
  • discover/runner.go keeps the candidate list honest: GPUDevices at line 36 returns refreshed devices with delta detection via sameRefreshDevice at 372, filters integrated GPUs at 382-435, and bootstraps driver libraries through a Metal retry path at 488 or a status watchdog at 564.
  • server/model.go is what gets loaded: parseFromModel at line 27 turns manifest layers into modelLayer entries, and detectChatTemplate at 99 picks the template that the runner will apply.

Why You Need This

Every local-inference tool eventually invents a memory manager, and comparing them is the fastest way to understand the design space. llama.cpp ships as a library and leaves residency policy to whoever embeds it; vLLM assumes a server with one big model and continuous batching, so its scheduler packs sequences, not models; and llamafile sidesteps the question by being a single self-contained binary for one model. Ollama’s situation is unique: a desktop daemon that must juggle chat models, embedding models, and vision models simultaneously on whatever hardware the user happens to own, with zero configuration. The answer in sched.go is a two-queue design - processPending at 274 for arrivals and processCompleted at 416 for departures - plus a reference-counted runner table. It is the same shape an operating system uses for process scheduling, applied to GPU residency, and reading it is a masterclass in resource management under uncertainty.

The eviction dance is the part worth studying twice. When a request arrives for a model that is not resident, the scheduler first checks whether the load can succeed: load() predicts VRAM at 585, picks a placement at 586, and, for the second-and-later model case, runs a pre-flight check at 598-605 that evicts before spawning if the prediction exceeds eighty percent of free memory at 601. If the load was tried and crashed with an OOM anyway, the OOM retry path at 365-375 evicts every resident model, waits for each unload to finish, and retries exactly once - a second crash falls through to fail-fast. Every eviction goes through the same ritual at 386-397: stop the expire timer, zero the session duration, and push the runner onto expiredCh once its reference count drains. The wisdom here is that OOM handling is separated into predicted-OOM (cheap, act early) and actual-OOM (expensive, recover once, then give up), a distinction most hand-rolled model servers get wrong by retrying forever against a wall that never moves.

The scheduler also quietly encodes years of community bug reports. The architecture list at 556-559 pins numParallel to 1 for model families that corrupt output under parallel decoding, with the issue number quoted in the comment; embedding models are forced to parallel 1 at 549-552 because there is nothing to batch; and vision models get their 2,048-token context floor at 223-226 because multimodal prompts genuinely do not fit below it. On the discovery side, integrated GPUs are filtered out unless explicitly admitted at 382-435 because iGPU memory reporting lied to earlier releases, and mmap is disabled under host memory pressure at 1242-1296 with a documented headroom constant at 1297. None of this is glamorous, and all of it is the difference between a tool that works on your machine and one that works on everyone’s machine - which is, ultimately, the only product Ollama sells.

Detail: routes feed a keyed runner table; the pending loop manages auto concurrency limits, free-space refresh, and placement; loads predict, clamp, and pre-flight; discovery filters and bootstraps devices; completions arm keep-alive timers.

The keep-alive story is subtler than the OLLAMA_KEEP_ALIVE env var suggests. When a request finishes, processCompleted at 416 decrements the runner’s refCount at 433 and, at zero, branches on session duration: zero means expire immediately at 434-441, while a positive duration arms a time.AfterFunc timer at 442-454 - and if a timer already exists, it is Reset rather than recreated at 455-458, with expiresAt recorded for status reporting. useLoadedRunner at 524 does the mirror image on arrival: increment refCount at 527, stop any pending expire timer at 528-531, and refresh sessionDuration from the request at 532-534 so a per-request keep_alive overrides the daemon default. The net effect is that a model stays warm exactly as long as the most recent request asked for, and the first byte of the next request never waits for weights to cross the PCIe bus. It is a tiny state machine - idle, referenced, expiring - but getting it wrong produces either VRAM exhaustion or the famous “model reloads every request” support thread.

Placement is the other half of the puzzle, and it reads like a tiny bin-packing solver with opinions. selectLlamaServerPlacement at 1014 first honors explicit placement hints, then considers a single-GPU fit at 1102 (preferred, because tensor parallelism across consumer GPUs is rarely worth the latency), then multi-GPU groups scored by betterPlacementGPU at 1120 and bestGPUGroupByAvailableMemory at 1128. The prediction feeding it comes from PredictServerVRAM at 585 using the context size computed by effectiveLlamaServerContext at 584 with numParallel folded in - which is why the parallel clamps at 546-559 matter for placement too. Two memory-shaping knobs then adjust the launch: automaticGenerationBatch at 875 sizes the decode batch to what the leftover VRAM can hold (generationBatchFits at 923, stepping down at 950-968 when it does not), and reduceAutoNumCtxForLoadOOM at 817 shrinks an auto-sized context on failure. mmap gets the same treatment at 1180-1296: defaults per OS, then a host-pressure override at 1242 with headroom at 1297, because on 32-GB machines the page cache is part of the memory story.

Discovery is the foundation the whole edifice stands on, and it is refreshingly defensive. GetSystemInfo at discover/gpu.go line 21 provides the baseline memory picture; GPUDevices at runner.go line 36 layers runtime detection on top, with sameRefreshDevice at 372 preventing spurious re-reporting between requests - important because the scheduler calls getGpuFn on every pending request at 325. Bootstrap is wrapped in failure recovery: bootstrapDevicesWithMetalRetry at 488 handles macOS driver hiccups, bootstrapDevicesWithStatusWatchdog at 564 guards the Windows/CUDA library path with a timeout, and filterOverlapByLibrary at 438 deduplicates devices that appear through multiple driver interfaces - the classic CUDA-plus-Vulkan double-count that once made users see twice the VRAM they owned. updateFreeSpace at sched.go 344 subtracts resident models from the picture, so the numbers the placement solver sees reflect what is actually free, not what the card shipped with.

The model layer closes the loop. parseFromModel at server/model.go line 27 resolves a name into manifest blobs and produces modelLayer entries - weights, projector, template - that detectChatTemplate at 99 post-processes; the gguf metadata that load() reads at 576 comes from the same files, giving the scheduler its model family, context training length, and tensor count before a single byte of VRAM is claimed. PullHandler at routes.go 1480 and CreateBlobHandler at 2209 maintain those blobs; ListHandler at 2131 reports what is installed. It is a clean separation: routes know names, model.go knows layers, sched.go knows memory, and discover knows hardware - four vocabularies meeting at one scheduler, which is exactly why a new backend can be added without touching the eviction logic.

From Install to a Warm Model

The README gets you running; the scheduler’s knobs are environment variables (commands abridged):

curl -fsSL https://ollama.com/install.sh | sh
ollama serve
# scheduler controls:
export OLLAMA_MAX_LOADED_MODELS=3      # resident model cap (auto = per-GPU default)
export OLLAMA_KEEP_ALIVE=10m           # default session duration per model
export OLLAMA_NUM_PARALLEL=2           # decode parallelism per runner
ollama run llama3.2 "hello"
ollama run nomic-embed-text "embed me"  # loads alongside, parallel=1 forced

Each loaded runner keeps its keep-alive timer reset on every request, so a model in steady use never unloads; stop talking and it expires exactly on schedule.

Honest limits: the scheduler is host-side only - it launches and monitors llama-server processes but does not batch across models, so two models share a GPU by time-slicing residency, not by compute interleaving; the VRAM predictor is an estimate, and exotic quantization mixes can still surprise it, which is why the fail-fast after one OOM retry exists; placement assumes homogeneous devices within a group and can misjudge split CPU+GPU layouts on unusual driver stacks; keep-alive timers are daemon-local, so a crash discards the residency policy along with the weights; and the whole design presumes one daemon per machine - multi-user GPU sharing is left to the tools built on top of it.
entry.summary: A source tour of Ollama's model scheduler: the pending-request loop, VRAM placement across multiple GPUs, pre-flight fit checks, OOM eviction and retry, keep-alive timers, and the device discovery that feeds them.
